title: Beyond straight lines
content:
Beyond straight lines# Every model so far was linear in its inputs, plus whatever products and powers we chose to add by hand (in Lecture 2 we had to decide to add \(G \times T\) or to take \(\ln V\)). This page introduces models that find the shape of a curve from the data: step functions, regression splines, smoothing splines, local regression and generalised additive models. The running example is the electricity demand of an office building through the day.
Notation on this page
Symbol Meaning \(x\) the input (here, the hour of the day, 0–24) \(d\) degree of a polynomial: its highest power of \(x\) bin one interval of the \(x\) axis in a step function knot a point on the \(x\) axis where one polynomial piece of a spline ends and the next begins cubic a polynomial of degree 3: \(a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3\) curvature how fast the slope changes: the second derivative \(K\) number of interior knots of a spline kW\(^2\) unit of the cross-validation error here (it is an MSE of a demand in kW) \(g(t)\), \(g''(t)\) a fitted curve, and its second derivative (curvature) at \(t\) \(\int \dots\, dt\) integral: adds up the quantity along the whole \(x\) range \(\lambda\) smoothing parameter: penalty on curvature \(x_0\) the point at which we want a prediction \(f_j(X_j)\) a curve (shape) for input \(j\) alone, fitted from the data Example: a building's electricity demand# A smart electricity meter records the demand every few minutes. Photo: RobbieIanMorrison, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 A smart meter records the power drawn by an office building. The demand is low at night, has a morning peak at about 9 am and a larger evening peak at about 7:30 pm. A load profile like this is what an energy manager or a utility wants to predict, for example to size a solar system or to plan tariffs. Our data are 120 readings taken at random times, and the goal is to predict the demand from the hour.
The 120 demand readings against the hour of the day: low at night, a morning peak near 9 am and a larger evening peak near 7:30 pm. The relation rises and falls twice; it is clearly not a straight line. Throughout this page, models are compared by their 10-fold cross-validation error (Lecture 4), in kW\(^2\). The noise variance, the best possible MSE, is 16 kW\(^2\).
Polynomials and step functions# Step functions jump at the bin edges; splines join smooth pieces at the knots. Polynomials. Add \(x^2, x^3, \dots, x^d\) as extra inputs (Lecture 2). This gives one formula for the whole day. A polynomial is global: changing the fit at 9 am changes it everywhere. A low degree is too stiff: a degree-4 polynomial has too few turning points to follow the night–peak–dip–peak–night shape. A high degree can follow it, but swings wildly near 0 h and 24 h, where data are few.
Step functions. Cut the day into bins and predict the average demand in each bin. This is simple, but the prediction jumps at the bin edges, and a peak that lies across two bins is smeared out.
model 10-fold CV error (kW\(^2\)) straight line 125.6 polynomial, degree 4 112.2 step function, 6 bins of 4 h 80.7 All three are far above the noise variance of 16.
Example: a step-function fit# Electricity demand (kW) was read at these hours:
hour 1 2 3 5 6 7 8 10 11 13 14 15 17 18 19 21 22 23 kW 18 16 17 30 44 52 49 33 28 24 26 31 45 58 61 40 30 22 Fit a step function with six 4-hour bins (0–4, 4–8, …, 20–24). What does it predict at 6:30 pm (hour 18.5) and at 9 am (hour 9)?
Solution triple-click to reveal A step function predicts the average of the readings in each bin:
bin 0–4 4–8 8–12 12–16 16–20 20–24 prediction (kW) 17.0 42.0 36.7 27.0 54.7 30.7 Hour 18.5 is in the 16–20 bin: 54.7 kW. Hour 9 is in the 8–12 bin: 36.7 kW, although the morning peak (about 50 kW at 7–8 h) is only an hour earlier: the bin edge at 8 h cuts the peak in two. This is the weakness that splines fix.
Regression splines# A regression spline combines the best of both:
Choose knots: points that cut the range of \(x\) into pieces. Fit a cubic polynomial (degree 3) in each piece. Force the pieces to join smoothly: at each knot, neighbouring pieces must have the same value, the same slope and the same curvature (second derivative). The joining conditions make the result look like one smooth curve. Each piece only has to follow its own part of the day, so there are no wild swings, and a change in one place stays local. A cubic spline with \(K\) interior knots has \(K + 4\) coefficients (ISLP Section 7.4).
A spline is still linear in the coefficients: it can be written as a sum of fixed basis functions (B-splines) times coefficients, so it is fitted by least squares exactly as in Lecture 2. In Python, scikit-learn's SplineTransformer turns the hour into B-spline columns and LinearRegression then fits them. (Its n_knots counts all knots, evenly spaced over the data, including the two ends.)
Natural splines A natural spline is also forced to be a straight line beyond the outer knots, which calms the behaviour at the ends of the range (ISLP Section 7.4.4).
Four fits of the same data# Four fits of the demand data: a straight line, a degree-4 polynomial, a step function, and a cubic spline with 9 knots. The dashed curve is the true demand (at 24 °C outdoors). The line and the polynomial miss both peaks; the steps are too coarse; the spline follows both peaks. The spline with 9 knots has a CV error of 30.3 kW\(^2\), four times smaller than the straight line. Most of the remaining gap (30 against the noise of 16) is the effect of outdoor temperature, which this model ignores; we add it below.
Choosing the form of the curve is part of the model. xkcd #2048 “Curve-Fitting” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. How many knots? Ask cross-validation# knots 10-fold CV error (kW\(^2\)) 4 51.5 5 72.3 6 29.9 9 30.3 12 29.1 25 33.7 Too few knots cannot follow the peaks. With few knots the result also depends on where the evenly spaced knots happen to fall relative to the peaks, which is why 5 knots does worse than 4. From 6 to about 15 knots the pieces are short enough to follow both peaks, and the fits are about equally good. Too many knots start to fit the noise. The number of knots is a flexibility setting, a hyperparameter, playing the role the polynomial degree played in Lecture 4, and it is chosen the same way: by cross-validation.
Two relatives: smoothing splines and local regression# Smoothing splines put a knot at every data point and control the wiggliness with a penalty on curvature. The fitted curve \(g\) minimises
\[ \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \int g''(t)^2\, dt . \]Here \(g''(t)\) is the second derivative (curvature) of \(g\) at \(t\), and the integral \(\int \dots\,dt\) adds up its square over the whole range of \(x\). The idea is the same as ridge regression (Lecture 4): \(\lambda = 0\) lets the curve pass through every point; \(\lambda \to \infty\) forces a straight line (which has zero curvature). \(\lambda\) is chosen by cross-validation (ISLP Section 7.5).
Local regression (also called LOESS) predicts at a point \(x_0\) by fitting a straight line to the nearby points only, weighted so that closer points count more, and then slides this window along \(x\). The width of the window, given as the fraction of points it contains (the span), controls the flexibility and is chosen by cross-validation (ISLP Section 7.6).
Generalised additive models (GAMs)# With several inputs, a generalised additive model gives each input its own shape and adds them together:
\[ Y = \beta_0 + f_1(X_1) + f_2(X_2) + \dots + f_p(X_p) + \varepsilon . \]A GAM replaces each term \(\beta_j X_j\) of linear regression by a flexible function \(f_j(X_j)\) (ISLP Section 7.7). Each \(f_j\) can be a spline, a straight line or a step function, and can be plotted and interpreted on its own. The price of “additive”: a GAM misses interactions between inputs unless we add them explicitly (for example, if the air conditioning only runs during office hours).
Building. Model the demand as a spline in the hour plus a straight line in the outdoor temperature:
\[ \text{demand} = f_1(\text{hour}) + \beta \times (\text{outdoor temperature}) . \] model 10-fold CV error (kW\(^2\)) spline in hour only 30.3 spline in hour + straight line in temperature 18.8 noise variance (best possible) 16 Adding the temperature removes most of the remaining error; the GAM is close to the best possible. The fitted slope \(\hat\beta = 0.82\) kW per \(^\circ\)C (true value 0.8) has a physical meaning: each extra degree outside costs about 0.8 kW of air conditioning.

title: Logistic regression
content:
Logistic regression# In Lectures 1 and 2 the output was mostly a number. Now the output is a category: a machine is healthy or faulty, a milk sample pure or adulterated, a sensor reading normal or an anomaly. This page develops the most widely used classifier, logistic regression: the model, how to read its coefficients, how it is fitted by maximum likelihood, and how its probabilities become decisions.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(Y\) output, coded 1 (“yes”, e.g. faulty) or 0 (“no”, e.g. healthy) \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) “probability of A given B” probability of \(A\) when \(B\) is known; a number from 0 (never) to 1 (certain) \(p(X)\) “p of X” \(\Pr(Y = 1 \mid X)\): probability that \(Y = 1\) for this value of the input \(X\) \(v\) RMS vibration velocity of a motor (mm/s) RMS “root mean square” \(\sqrt{\text{mean of the squared signal}}\): the typical size of an oscillating signal \(\sigma(z)\) “sigma of z” the logistic (sigmoid) function \(1/(1 + e^{-z})\); not the noise \(\sigma\) of earlier lectures \(e\) Euler's number, 2.718…; \(e^{-z}\) is the exponential function \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) intercept and slope of the straight line inside the sigmoid odds \(p/(1 - p)\): probability of yes divided by probability of no \(\ln\) natural logarithm; \(\ln[p/(1-p)]\) is the log-odds, also called the logit \(q\) probability of heads for a coin (the parameter in the likelihood example) \(L\) likelihood: the probability of the observed data, for given parameter values \(p_i\) model probability that observation \(i\) has \(Y = 1\): \(p_i = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)\) \(\prod\) “product” (capital pi) multiply the terms together, as \(\sum\) adds them \(\ell_i\), \(J(\boldsymbol\beta)\) loss of observation \(i\); cost (average loss) for coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) \(\mathbf y\), \(\mathbf p\) columns of observed outcomes (0s and 1s) and of predicted probabilities \(p_i\) \(\alpha\) “alpha” step size of gradient descent \(\hat p(v)\) “p hat” fitted probability of a fault at vibration \(v\) \(z\) here: estimate divided by its standard error (read like the \(t\) of Lecture 2) \(T\) bearing temperature (\(^\circ\)C) Classification problems# An electric motor. Is it healthy or developing a fault? A classification question. Photo: Rama, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 fr Typical classification problems in physics and instrumentation:
Is a machine healthy or faulty? Is a milk sample pure or adulterated? Is a sensor reading normal, or an anomaly? Which fault does a machine have: imbalance, misalignment or bearing wear? The first three have two classes; the last has three (more than two classes are treated on the generative models page).
With two classes we code the output as \(Y = 1\) (“yes”, usually the class we want to detect, e.g. faulty) or \(Y = 0\) (“no”, e.g. healthy). Rather than a bare yes or no, we want the probability that \(Y = 1\):
\[ p(X) = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid X). \]The vertical bar is read “given”: \(\Pr(Y = 1 \mid X)\) is the probability that \(Y = 1\) for this value of \(X\). The probability changes with the inputs: a motor vibrating at 6 mm/s has a different probability of a fault from one at 2 mm/s.
Classification therefore has two separate steps, and keeping them apart is the key idea of this lecture:
Estimate the probability of each class. Turn the probability into a decision, using a threshold that depends on the costs of the possible mistakes. Example: vibration and motor faults# A motor with a worn bearing or a loose mounting vibrates more. Vibration monitoring is the standard tool of predictive maintenance: an accelerometer on the motor housing measures how strongly it shakes. The severity is usually reported as the RMS (root-mean-square) vibration velocity \(v\) in mm/s, the typical speed of the vibrating surface, which is the quantity used in the ISO vibration-severity standards.
Our data: 200 motors, with input \(X = v\) and output \(Y = 1\) if the motor was faulty, 0 if healthy. 114 of the 200 are faulty.
The 200 motors: each mark is one motor, placed at its vibration level; faulty motors in the top row (\(Y = 1\)), healthy ones in the bottom row (\(Y = 0\)). Below about 3 mm/s all motors are healthy; above about 5 mm/s nearly all are faulty; in between there is a grey zone where both occur. Why not use linear regression?# We could treat 0 and 1 as numbers and fit a least-squares line, as in Lecture 2. For the motors this gives
\[ \hat y = -0.15 + 0.144\,v . \]A straight line (red) fitted to the 0/1 motor data. The shaded regions, below 0 and above 1, are impossible values for a probability, and the line enters both. At \(v = 0\) the line predicts \(-0.15\); at \(v = 10\) mm/s it predicts \(-0.15 + 0.144 \times 10 = 1.29\). Neither is a possible probability. A straight line also rises at the same rate everywhere, while the real probability is flat near 0, rises steeply in the grey zone, and is flat again near 1. We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1.
A straight line fitted to 0/1 data predicts impossible probabilities; the logistic curve stays between 0 and 1. The logistic (sigmoid) function# The logistic function, also called the sigmoid (“S-shaped”), is
\[ \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} , \]where \(e = 2.718\ldots\) is Euler's number. Note that the Greek letter \(\sigma\) here names a function; it has nothing to do with the noise standard deviation \(\sigma\) of earlier lectures.
The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\): an S-shaped curve that rises from 0 to 1 and passes through 0.5 at \(z = 0\). Its properties:
Any number \(z\) can go in, and the output is always between 0 and 1. \(e^{-z}\) is always positive, so the denominator is always greater than 1 and the fraction lies between 0 and 1. \(z = 0\) gives \(\sigma(0) = 1/(1 + e^0) = 1/2\). Large positive \(z\) gives a value close to 1: \(\sigma(4) = 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 1/1.018 = 0.982\). Large negative \(z\) gives a value close to 0: \(\sigma(-4) = 1/(1 + 54.6) = 0.018\). The logistic regression model# Logistic regression in one picture: a straight-line score, squeezed by the sigmoid into a probability, then a threshold. Put a straight line inside the sigmoid:
\[ p(X) = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X)}} . \]The linear part \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X\) is the same as in Lecture 2 and can be any number; the sigmoid squeezes it into a probability between 0 and 1.
If \(\beta_1 > 0\), \(p\) rises with \(X\); if \(\beta_1 < 0\), it falls. The steepness of the S is set by \(\beta_1\): a large \(\beta_1\) gives a sharp step, a small one a gentle slope. The position of the S is where the line crosses zero, because \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\): \(p = 0.5\) at \(X = -\beta_0/\beta_1\). Two logistic curves. Blue: \(\beta_0 = -10\), \(\beta_1 = 2.5\), crossing 0.5 at \(X = 10/2.5 = 4\). Green: \(\beta_0 = -4\), \(\beta_1 = 0.8\), a gentler curve crossing 0.5 at \(X = 4/0.8 = 5\). Try it. Move \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) until the curve follows the 0/1 data, then press Maximum likelihood. The 50% point is where the classifier switches. Odds and log-odds# The odds are the probability of yes divided by the probability of no:
\[ \text{odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p} . \]\(p = 0.5\) gives odds of 1 (“evens”); \(p = 0.8\) gives odds of \(0.8/0.2 = 4\) (“four to one”). Odds run from 0 to \(\infty\).
For logistic regression, the logarithm of the odds, the log-odds or logit, is a straight line in \(X\):
\[ \ln\frac{p}{1 - p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X . \]So logistic regression is linear regression for the log-odds.
From \(p\) to the log-odds From \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) we get \(1 - p = e^{-z}/(1 + e^{-z})\), so \(p/(1 - p) = 1/e^{-z} = e^{z}\) and therefore \(\ln[p/(1 - p)] = z\).
Reading \(\beta_1\). Increase \(X\) by 1 and the log-odds increase by \(\beta_1\). Adding \(\beta_1\) to a logarithm multiplies the quantity by \(e^{\beta_1}\), so the odds are multiplied by \(e^{\beta_1}\). Note that it is the odds, not the probability, that change by a fixed factor.
Example: probability, odds and log-odds# A fitted model for motor faults is \(\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = -6 + 1.5\,x\), with \(x\) the vibration level (mm/s). (a) Find the probability of a fault at \(x = 5\). (b) At which vibration is the probability 50%? (c) By what factor do the odds grow for each extra 1 mm/s?
Solution triple-click to reveal (a) \(z = -6 + 1.5 \times 5 = 1.5\), so \(p = 1/(1 + e^{-1.5}) = 0.818\). The odds are \(e^{1.5} = 4.48\).
(b) \(p = 0.5\) when \(z = 0\): \(x = 6/1.5 = 4\) mm/s.
(c) The log-odds rise by 1.5 per mm/s, so the odds are multiplied by \(e^{1.5} = 4.48\).
What is a likelihood?# Before fitting logistic regression we need one new idea, shown first with a coin, where the answer is obvious.
The likelihood \(L\) is the probability of getting the data we actually observed, if the model's parameters had a given value. The data are fixed (they have been measured); the parameter is what we vary. For each possible parameter value, the likelihood says how probable our actual data would have been.
Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters that make the observed data most probable. It is the principle behind most fitting methods in this course.
Example: a coin. Ten tosses give 7 heads and 3 tails. Let \(q\) be the probability of heads. Each head has probability \(q\) and each tail \(1 - q\); the tosses are independent, so the probabilities multiply:
\[ L(q) = q^7 (1 - q)^3 . \] \(q\) 0.5 0.7 0.9 \(L(q)\) 0.0010 0.0022 0.0005 The likelihood is largest at \(\hat q = 0.7\), the obvious answer: the fraction of heads, 7 out of 10.
Worked numbers
\(0.5^7 \times 0.5^3 = 0.5^{10} = 0.000977\). \(0.7^7 \times 0.3^3 = 0.0824 \times 0.027 = 0.00222\). \(0.9^7 \times 0.1^3 = 0.478 \times 0.001 = 0.00048\).
Why \(\hat q = 7/10\) exactly \(\ln L = 7\ln q + 3\ln(1 - q)\). Its derivative \(7/q - 3/(1 - q)\) is zero when \(7(1 - q) = 3q\), so \(q = 0.7\).
Fitting logistic regression by maximum likelihood# For given coefficients, the model assigns each motor \(i\) a probability of being faulty, \(p_i = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 v_i)\). The probability of what actually happened to that motor is \(p_i\) if it was faulty (\(y_i = 1\)) and \(1 - p_i\) if it was healthy (\(y_i = 0\)).
The motors are independent, so the probability of the whole data set, the likelihood, is the product over all motors:
\[ L(\boldsymbol\beta) = \prod_{i:\,y_i = 1} p_i \ \times \prod_{i:\,y_i = 0} \bigl(1 - p_i\bigr). \]The symbol \(\prod\) (capital Greek pi) means “multiply together”, just as \(\sum\) means “add up”; \(\prod_{i:\,y_i = 1}\) runs over the motors that were faulty. Good coefficients give a high \(p_i\) to faulty motors and a low \(p_i\) to healthy ones, which makes \(L\) large. Maximum likelihood chooses the \(\beta\)'s that make \(L\) as large as possible, exactly as with the coin. The only difference is that the coin had one parameter, while here there are two, and each motor has its own probability \(p_i\).
(Least squares in Lecture 2 is also maximum likelihood, when the noise is Gaussian; ESL Section 2.6.3.)
Loss and cost: cross-entropy# In the loss-and-cost language of gradient descent, the loss of one motor is minus the logarithm of the probability the model gave to what really happened:
\[ \ell_i = \begin{cases} -\ln p_i & \text{if faulty } (y_i = 1),\\ -\ln(1 - p_i) & \text{if healthy } (y_i = 0). \end{cases} \]The cost is the average loss, which equals \(-\frac1n \ln L\):
\[ J(\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac1n \sum_i \Bigl[\, y_i \ln p_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - p_i) \Bigr]. \]Since \(y_i\) is 0 or 1, only one of the two terms is non-zero for each motor (when \(y_i = 1\), the second term has the factor \(1 - y_i = 0\), and vice versa), so this one formula covers both cases. The logarithm turns the product \(L\) into a sum, which is easier to compute and avoids numbers too small for the computer; the minus sign turns maximising into minimising; and \(\frac1n\) makes it an average. Minimising this cost is the same as maximising the likelihood. It is called the cross-entropy or log loss (the name comes from information theory), and it also trains neural-network classifiers (Lecture 7).
Confident mistakes are punished heavily. For one faulty motor:
model's \(p_i\) situation loss \(-\ln p_i\) 0.99 confident and right 0.01 0.5 unsure \(\ln 2 = 0.69\) 0.01 confident and wrong 4.6 Example: the cost of a confident mistake# For one machine the model gives \(p = 0.9\) for “faulty”. Compute the cross-entropy loss \(-[y\ln p + (1-y)\ln(1-p)]\) if the machine really is faulty (\(y = 1\)) and if it is healthy (\(y = 0\)).
Solution triple-click to reveal \(y = 1\): loss \(= -\ln 0.9 = 0.105\). Small: the model was confident and right.
\(y = 0\): loss \(= -\ln(1 - 0.9) = -\ln 0.1 = 2.303\). About 22 times larger: a confident wrong answer is punished hard.
Gradient descent for logistic regression# Setting the derivatives of \(J\) to zero gives equations that cannot be solved by algebra: there is no formula for the best \(\boldsymbol\beta\). So we walk downhill with gradient descent. The gradient of the cross-entropy is \(-\frac1n\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf p)\), where \(\mathbf y\) is the column of observed outcomes and \(\mathbf p\) the column of predicted probabilities, so the update is
\[ \boldsymbol\beta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\beta + \frac{\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\bigl(\mathbf y - \mathbf p\bigr). \]Compare it with linear regression:
\[ \boldsymbol\beta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\beta + \frac{\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\bigl(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\bigr). \]It is the same rule: the step is proportional to (measured \(-\) predicted) \(\times\) input. Only the prediction changes, a probability instead of a straight line. For example \(y = 1\) with \(p = 0.3\) gives an error of 0.7. The similarity is not a coincidence: both rules come from maximum likelihood.
Motors. At the start all coefficients are zero, so every \(p_i = 0.5\) and the cost is \(\ln 2 = 0.693\). After 3000 steps (standardised input, \(\alpha = 1\)) the cost is 0.140. LogisticRegression in scikit-learn gives the same answer, using a faster (Newton-type) method.
Switching off regularisation in scikit-learn By default scikit-learn's LogisticRegression adds a penalty on large coefficients (regularisation, Lecture 4). Use C=np.inf to switch it off, so that the result is pure maximum likelihood, as in ISLP.
Motors: the result# The maximum-likelihood fit is
\[ \hat p(v) = \sigma(-10.1 + 2.39\,v). \]The fitted probability of a fault, \(\hat p(v)\) (blue curve), and the fraction of motors that were faulty in each 1-mm/s bin (red dots; for example, 62% of the motors between 4 and 5 mm/s were faulty). The curve passes through the dots. 50% point: where the line inside the sigmoid is zero, \(-10.1 + 2.39\,v = 0\), so \(v = 4.2\) mm/s. (The true value in the simulation is 4.0 mm/s.) Odds: each extra mm/s multiplies the odds of a fault by \(e^{2.39} = 10.9\). Is the effect real? As in Lecture 2, each coefficient has a standard error (SE). Here \(\hat\beta_1 = 2.39\), SE \(= 0.45\), and the ratio, called \(z\) for logistic regression, is \(z = 2.39/0.45 = 5.3\). \(|z| > 2\), so the effect is real. In maintenance terms: below 2 mm/s the chance of a fault is under 1%; above 6 mm/s it is over 98%. Worked numbers
50% point: \(10.10/2.386 = 4.24\) mm/s. Odds factor: \(e^{2.386} = 10.9\). \(z = 2.386/0.452 = 5.3\).
\(\hat p(2) = \sigma(-10.10 + 4.77) = \sigma(-5.33) = 0.005\); \(\hat p(6) = \sigma(-10.10 + 14.32) = \sigma(4.22) = 0.985\).
Where the standard errors come from \(\mathrm{SE}^2\) is the diagonal of \((\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\), where \(\mathbf W\) is a diagonal matrix with entries \(W_{ii} = p_i(1 - p_i)\) (ESL Section 4.4.1).
From a probability to a decision# To classify, choose a threshold, the probability above which we say “faulty”. The usual choice is 0.5: predict \(Y = 1\) if \(\hat p \ge 0.5\), i.e. predict the more probable class.
Because \(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\) exactly when \(z \ge 0\), the condition \(\hat p \ge 0.5\) is the same as \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X \ge 0\). The decision boundary, the set of input values where the decision changes, is therefore where \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X = 0\). For the motors it is \(v = 4.2\) mm/s: motors above it are called faulty.
Logistic regression gives a probability; the threshold turns it into a yes/no decision. We are free to choose the threshold, and 0.5 is not always best: the next page, How good is a classifier?, shows how to choose it.
Two inputs: the decision boundary is a line# A monitoring system records two inputs for each machine: the vibration \(v\) (mm/s) and the bearing temperature \(T\) (\(^\circ\)C). A failing bearing both vibrates and heats up through friction, so using both sensors should classify better than either alone. We have 400 training machines (122 faulty) and, kept apart, 2000 test machines (593 faulty); every performance number on the next pages is measured on the test machines.
The 400 training machines (simulated): bearing temperature against vibration. Healthy machines form a compact cloud; faulty ones run hotter and vibrate more, and their cloud is more spread out and stretched along a diagonal, because in faulty machines high vibration and high temperature go together. The two groups overlap, so some errors are unavoidable. Logistic regression with two inputs gives
\[ \hat p = \sigma(-15.8 + 1.28\,v + 0.199\,T). \]The boundary \(\hat p = 0.5\) is where \(-15.8 + 1.28\,v + 0.199\,T = 0\). Solving for \(T\):
\[ T = 79.6 - 6.41\,v , \]a straight line. Machines above the line are classified faulty, those below it healthy. A machine at 2 mm/s is called faulty above \(79.6 - 12.8 = 66.8\) \(^\circ\)C; at 5 mm/s, above 47.5 \(^\circ\)C. High vibration and high temperature can each push a machine over the line.
The logistic-regression decision boundary \(T = 79.6 - 6.41\,v\) drawn over the training machines: above the line, faulty; below, healthy. Worked numbers
Dividing the boundary equation by 0.1991: \(15.84/0.1991 = 79.6\); \(1.276/0.1991 = 6.41\).

title: Neural networks
content:
Neural networks# With SVMs, splines and trees, a person chooses the inputs. Neural networks can start from raw measurements (pixels, samples of a signal) and build useful features themselves in their hidden layers. A network is assembled from pieces met in earlier lectures: linear models, the sigmoid, loss and cost, gradient descent and the ridge penalty. This page puts them together, explains how a network is trained (backpropagation), and shows how to stop it overfitting.
Notation on this page
Symbol Meaning \(X_j\) input \(j\), \(j = 1, \dots, p\) \(A_k\) activation (output) of hidden unit \(k\) \(w_{kj}\) weight from input \(j\) to hidden unit \(k\) \(w_{k0}\) bias of hidden unit \(k\): its intercept (not the “bias” of the bias–variance trade-off) \(g\) activation function, a non-linear function applied by each hidden unit \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_k\) bias of the output, and weight of hidden unit \(k\) in the output \(f(X)\) the network's prediction \(z\) the number fed into an activation function ReLU rectified linear unit, \(g(z) = \max(0, z)\): \(z\) if positive, otherwise 0 \(a\), \(b\) numbers of units in two consecutive layers parameters all the weights and biases: what training finds minibatch a small random set of rows used for one gradient-descent step epoch one pass through all the training data seed the number that fixes the random starting weights \(\lambda\), \(w\) penalty strength and weights in weight decay A network with one hidden layer# The Mark I Perceptron (1958): the first neural network, built in hardware. Photo: John C. Hay, Albert E. Murray, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain One neuron: weight the inputs, add them, pass the result through an activation. A hidden unit (or neuron) \(k\) computes a linear model of the inputs and passes it through a non-linear activation function \(g\):
\[ A_k = g\Bigl(w_{k0} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_{kj} X_j\Bigr). \]The numbers \(w_{kj}\) are its weights and \(w_{k0}\) its bias (intercept); they are learned from the data. The network's output is then a linear model in the hidden units (ISLP equation 10.1):
\[ f(X) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k} \beta_k A_k . \]For classification, a sigmoid is applied to \(f\) to give a probability, as in logistic regression.
A network with inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_4\), one hidden layer of units \(A_1, \dots, A_5\) and an output \(f\). Every input connects to every hidden unit, and every hidden unit to the output: a fully connected (dense) network. The layer is called hidden because it is neither input nor output: we never observe the values \(A_k\).
Example: a forward pass by hand# A network has 2 inputs, 2 hidden ReLU units and one linear output: \(h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 + 2x_2)\), \(h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-x_1 + 0.5x_2 + 1)\), \(\hat y = 1.5h_1 - 2h_2 + 0.5\). Compute \(\hat y\) for \(\mathbf x = (0.5, -1)\). (ReLU is defined in the next section: \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\).)
Solution triple-click to reveal \(h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(0.5 - 2) = \mathrm{ReLU}(-1.5) = 0\).
\(h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-0.5 - 0.5 + 1) = \mathrm{ReLU}(0) = 0\).
\(\hat y = 1.5(0) - 2(0) + 0.5 = 0.5\). Both hidden units are switched off here, so only the output bias is left.
Activation functions# The three most common activation functions. Two activation functions matter most:
the sigmoid, \(g(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\), from Lecture 3; the ReLU (rectified linear unit), \(g(z) = \max(0, z)\): it passes positive values unchanged and sets negative ones to zero. It is fast and is the usual choice today. Its slope is either 1 or 0, which keeps training fast in deep networks, whereas the sigmoid's slope becomes tiny for large \(|z|\). Why must \(g\) be non-linear? A linear function of a linear function is linear. Without \(g\), a network would be just one big linear model, however many layers it had. The non-linearity is what lets the network bend and combine.
The sigmoid (an S-curve from 0 to 1) and the ReLU (zero for negative \(z\), equal to \(z\) for positive \(z\)). Try it. Change the weight and the bias, then switch between sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. The weight sets how sharp the switch is; the bias moves it. Many layers# A network with two hidden layers: every unit feeds every unit of the next layer. A deep network stacks hidden layers: each layer's outputs are the next layer's inputs. Early layers compute simple features; later layers compute combinations of them. (In image networks, early layers respond to edges and spots, later ones to shapes made of them.)
The output layer depends on the task:
one unit with a sigmoid for a yes/no classification; \(K\) units with a softmax for \(K\) classes (Lecture 3); one plain unit (no activation) for regression. Counting parameters. A fully connected layer from \(a\) units to \(b\) units has \(a \times b\) weights plus \(b\) biases. For example, a network with 6 inputs, two hidden layers of 64 units, and 1 output has
\[ \underbrace{6 \times 64 + 64}_{448} + \underbrace{64 \times 64 + 64}_{4160} + \underbrace{64 \times 1 + 1}_{65} = 4673 \text{ parameters}, \]against 7 for logistic regression on the same 6 inputs.
Example: counting parameters# A network for the six-sensor machines has 6 inputs, a hidden layer of 32 units, a second hidden layer of 16 units, and 1 output. How many weights and biases does it learn? Compare with logistic regression on the same inputs.
Solution triple-click to reveal Each layer has (inputs × units) weights plus one bias per unit:
6 → 32: \(6 \times 32 + 32 = 224\) 32 → 16: \(32 \times 16 + 16 = 528\) 16 → 1: \(16 \times 1 + 1 = 17\) Total 769 parameters, against 7 for logistic regression. With a few hundred machines that is a lot: regularisation and early stopping matter.
Fitting a network# A network is fitted like the models of Lectures 2 and 3:
Loss: squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification. Gradient descent, with two additions: backpropagation, which uses the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, working backwards from the output; minibatches: each step uses a small random batch of rows (e.g. 64) instead of all the data. One pass through all the training data is an epoch; with 2000 rows and batches of 64, one epoch is 32 steps. Unlike linear and logistic regression, the cost is not a single bowl: it has many valleys, and different random starting weights (fixed by the seed) give different networks. There is no guarantee of finding the best answer, but in practice many valleys are about equally good.
Backpropagation# Forward pass to compute the loss; backward pass (the chain rule) to compute every gradient. “Backpropagation” sounds frightening, but it is the chain rule of calculus plus careful bookkeeping. Recall the chain rule: the derivative of \(f(g(x))\) is \(f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\). For example, the derivative of \((3x + 1)^2\) is \(2(3x + 1) \times 3\).
One training step:
Forward pass: feed a minibatch through the network, layer by layer, to get the predictions. Loss: compare the predictions with the true outputs. Backward pass: start at the output and go back layer by layer, using the chain rule to find how much each weight changed the loss: its gradient. Update: move every weight a small step against its gradient (gradient descent). Repeat with the next minibatch. For an output weight, the gradient is (error) \(\times\) (the hidden unit's value), just as in linear regression. For a weight one layer further down, the chain rule multiplies by the output weight and by the slope of the activation \(g\). Why “back”? A weight in an early layer affects the loss only through the later layers, so its gradient is built from the later layers' gradients, which are computed first and reused. The whole backward pass costs about as much as one forward pass (ISLP Section 10.7).
Worked numbers: one forward and backward pass
One input \(x = 2\), one hidden ReLU unit with weight \(w = 0.5\), output weight \(\beta = 3\), target \(y = 1\), loss \(\frac12(y - \hat y)^2\).
Forward: \(A = \max(0, 0.5 \times 2) = 1\); \(\hat y = 3 \times 1 = 3\); loss \(= \frac12(1 - 3)^2 = 2\).
Backward: \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial\hat y = \hat y - y = 2\); \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial\beta = 2 \times A = 2\); \(\partial\text{loss}/\partial w = 2 \times \beta \times g'(1) \times x = 2 \times 3 \times 1 \times 2 = 12\) (the ReLU's slope \(g'\) is 1 for positive input).
In PyTorch, the most widely used deep-learning library, loss.backward() performs step 3 and optimizer.step() step 4. The usual optimiser is Adam, a version of gradient descent that adapts the step size for each weight from its recent gradients; it needs little tuning.
Six-sensor machines again# The six-sensor machines of Lecture 5, now with 2000 training machines. All networks were trained for 200 epochs. The best possible error is about 0.05 (5% of the labels are random).
Model parameters training error test error Logistic regression 7 0.146 0.149 Network, 1 hidden layer of 16 129 0.086 0.099 Network, 2 hidden layers of 64 4673 0.000 0.125 Network, 2 × 64, with dropout 4673 0.049 0.080 Random forest (300 trees) 0.048 The big network memorises the training data: training error 0, including the 5% of labels that are random. That is a sure sign of overfitting. Dropout (explained below) helps a lot: from 0.125 to 0.080. The random forest still wins on this table of sensor readings; its 0.048 is at the floor. The fault rules are thresholds, which trees represent exactly, while a network must build them out of smooth pieces. Worked numbers
16 hidden units: \(6 \times 16 + 16 = 112\), plus \(16 + 1 = 17\): 129 parameters. A network with no hidden layer and a sigmoid output has \(6 + 1 = 7\) parameters: it is exactly logistic regression, and gives the same test error, 0.149.
Try it. Press Train and watch a small network learn a boundary no straight line can draw. Try 1 hidden unit, then 8. Overfitting as training goes on# Stop training when the validation loss stops falling. The 2 × 64 network without dropout, recorded every 10 epochs: the training loss falls towards 0, while the test error is lowest early (0.097 at epoch 10) and then rises to about 0.12. The training loss falls from 0.25 at epoch 10 to 0.004 at epoch 170. The test error is 0.097, 0.102, 0.113, 0.120 and 0.124 at epochs 10, 50, 90, 130 and 170: the longer the network trains, the more noise it fits.
Early stopping uses this: keep back a validation set from the training data, and stop training when the error on it stops improving. (The plot uses the test set only to show the effect. In practice the validation set decides when to stop, and the test set is used once, at the end.)
A trained network is only as good as what it was trained on. xkcd #2173 “Trained a Neural Net” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Regularising a network# Networks have many parameters, so they almost always need at least one of these:
Dropout: during training, switch off each hidden unit at random (here 30% of the time), so that no unit can rely on another. At prediction time all units are used, with their weights scaled to match. Dropout acts like training many thinned networks and averaging them, similar to bagging (Lecture 5). Weight decay: add \(\lambda\sum w^2\) to the loss, where \(w\) runs over the weights and \(\lambda\) is the penalty strength. This is ridge regression (Lecture 4) for networks. Early stopping: stop training when the validation error is lowest.

title: Principal components analysis
content:
Principal components analysis# In Lectures 2–7 every example had an output \(Y\) to predict: that is supervised learning. In unsupervised learning there are only inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_p\), and no right answer to check against. That makes results harder to judge (there is no test error), so they must be checked against knowledge of the problem. There are two main goals:
summarise many variables with a few: principal components analysis (this page); find groups of similar objects: clustering. Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(X_j\) standardised sensor \(j\) (mean 0, variance 1) \(p\) number of variables (8 sensors) \(Z_m\) the \(m\)-th principal component, a combination of the sensors \(\phi_{jm}\) “phi j m” loading: the weight of sensor \(j\) in component \(m\) \(z_{im}\) score: the value of component \(m\) for reading \(i\) \(\sum_j \phi_{j1}^2 = 1\) fixes the size of the loadings, so only their direction matters \(r\) correlation coefficient: near \(\pm 1\) for variables that rise and fall together, 0 for uncorrelated ones PVE proportion of variance explained by a component \(z_j\), \(\hat z_j\) “z j”, “z j hat” standardised value of sensor \(j\) in a new reading; the same value rebuilt from the component scores AUC area under the ROC curve (Lecture 3): 1 = perfect, 0.5 = guessing Example: a pump station# A pumping station whose sensors usually move together. Photo: Rhododendrites, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 A water pump at a utility is monitored by 8 sensors: flow, discharge pressure, suction pressure, motor current, motor power, and bearing, motor and oil temperatures. This is a typical record from a SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) system. We have 500 readings of normal operation.
There are eight numbers per reading, but they move together. When the pump works harder, flow, pressure, current and power all rise (they are correlated); when the day is hot, all the temperatures rise. How many things are really changing?
The idea of principal components analysis (PCA): find a few new variables, combinations of the 8 sensors, that capture most of the variation.
Standardise first. The sensors have different units. Without standardising, the sensor with the largest numbers (for example pressure in kPa) would dominate the variance. After standardising, each sensor has variance 1, so the total variance of the 8 sensors is 8.
Principal components# PCA finds the direction of largest spread, then the next one at right angles. The first principal component is the combination
\[ Z_1 = \phi_{11} X_1 + \phi_{21} X_2 + \dots + \phi_{p1} X_p \]with the largest variance, subject to \(\sum_j \phi_{j1}^2 = 1\). (Without that constraint the variance could be made as large as we like by multiplying all the \(\phi\)'s by a big number.)
The second principal component \(Z_2\) is the combination with the largest variance among those uncorrelated with \(Z_1\); the third is uncorrelated with both; and so on. There are at most \(p\) components.
Two words:
the loadings \(\phi_{jm}\) say how much each sensor contributes to component \(m\); the scores \(z_{im}\) are the values of component \(m\) for each reading \(i\). Geometrically, the readings form a cloud of points in 8 dimensions. PC1 is the direction in which the cloud is most stretched, its longest axis; PC2 is the next longest axis, at right angles to the first.
The mathematics The loading vectors are the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix of the data, and the variances of the components are the corresponding eigenvalues (ESL Section 14.5.1).
Try it. Turn the direction. The orange dots are the points projected onto the line; their spread is the variance along that direction. PC1 makes it as large as possible; PC2 is at right angles. How much does each component explain?# The proportion of variance explained (PVE) by a component is its variance divided by the total variance (8 here).
A scree plot: the variance explained by each component (bars) and the cumulative total (line). PC1 explains 69.8%, PC2 22.8%, and PC3 to PC8 only 1–2% each (noise). A plot like this is called a scree plot (scree is the pile of rubble at the foot of a cliff: the small components after the drop). Look for the elbow, where the curve bends and flattens and later components add little. Here two components explain \(69.8 + 22.8 = 92.6\%\) of the variation.
Worked numbers
PC1's variance is \(0.698 \times 8 = 5.6\) standardised sensors' worth. Each noise component has about \(0.012 \times 8 = 0.1\), close to the noise variance per standardised sensor.
Example: proportion of variance explained# A PCA of five standardised pump-station sensors gives the component variances (eigenvalues) 2.7, 1.2, 0.6, 0.3 and 0.2. Compute the proportion of variance explained by each component and the cumulative proportion. How many components keep at least 90%?
Solution triple-click to reveal The total variance of five standardised inputs is 5.0 (one per input), and indeed \(2.7 + 1.2 + 0.6 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 5.0\). Dividing each variance by 5.0:
component 1 2 3 4 5 PVE 0.54 0.24 0.12 0.06 0.04 cumulative 0.54 0.78 0.90 0.96 1.00 Three components keep 90% (two keep only 78%): three numbers per reading instead of five.
What do the components mean? The loadings# Loadings of the 8 sensors on PC1 and PC2. PC1 = “load”. Flow \(+0.38\), discharge pressure \(+0.39\), current \(+0.39\) and power \(+0.39\) rise together, and suction pressure (\(-0.37\)) falls: a pump drawing more water lowers the pressure at its inlet. The temperatures also load positively (\(+0.23\) to \(+0.33\)). PC2 = “temperature”. The three temperatures load strongly (\(+0.42\) to \(+0.59\)), against the hydraulic and electrical sensors (\(-0.18\) to \(-0.27\)); suction pressure has \(+0.25\). So there are eight sensors, but only two things really change: how hard the pump works, and how warm it is. These are exactly the two hidden factors used to simulate the data.
The scores: each reading as two numbers# The 500 normal readings plotted by their scores on PC1 (load) and PC2 (temperature). Each dot is one reading of all 8 sensors. A plot of 2 numbers instead of 8 is easy to watch on a control-room screen. The scores can also be used as the inputs of a regression (principal components regression): with many correlated inputs, regressing on a few components is an alternative to ridge and lasso (ISLP Section 6.3.1).
Monitoring with PCA# Learn what normal looks like; a reading far from it is an anomaly. Normal readings lie close to the plane of PC1 and PC2: 92.6% of the variation is in that plane, and the rest is small noise. This gives a way to detect faults.
Reconstruction error. Project a new reading onto the 2 components, rebuild the 8 standardised sensor values \(\hat z_j\) from the 2 scores, and measure how far off they are:
\[ \text{error} = \sum_{j=1}^{8} \bigl(z_j - \hat z_j\bigr)^2 . \]Geometrically this is the squared distance from the reading to the plane (in process monitoring it is called the \(Q\) or SPE statistic). A large error means the sensors no longer agree with each other.
Example: a partial blockage. Normally motor current and flow rise together. A blockage makes the motor work harder for less water: current up, flow down. Each sensor on its own may look normal, but together they break the usual pattern.
We test this on 900 new normal readings and 100 readings with a blockage:
alarm based on AUC the most extreme single sensor 0.75 PCA reconstruction error 0.99 Set the alarm threshold at the 99th percentile of the error on the 500 normal training readings (the value only 1% of normal readings exceed; here 1.66). Then 88% of blockages are caught, with 1.3% false alarms on new normal readings.
No fault labels were needed: the monitor was built from normal data only, and flags anything that does not look normal. That is valuable when faults are rare and varied, as in most plants: it is a method for anomaly detection and early fault detection from sensor data.

title: Resampling
content:
Resampling# The rule of Lecture 1 is to choose a model by its test error. With simulated data we could generate thousands of new test points. A real project usually has one data set, often small. This page shows how to estimate the test error from that one data set by cross-validation, and how to find the uncertainty of almost any estimate by the bootstrap. Both work by resampling: reusing the data we have in different ways.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning MSE mean squared error \(\frac1n\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\); units of \(y\) squared \(R\) thermistor resistance (k\(\Omega\)) \(T\), \(T_K\) temperature in \(^\circ\)C; the same in kelvin, \(T_K = T + 273.15\) \(x = \ln R\) the input: natural logarithm of the resistance \(d\) degree (highest power of \(x\)) of a polynomial; a hyperparameter \(B\) thermistor constant (3950 K) in the physics section; number of bootstrap samples in the bootstrap section \(n\) number of data points (40 thermistor readings) \(\hat y_{(-i)}\) “y hat minus i” prediction for point \(i\) from the model fitted without point \(i\) \(\mathrm{MSE}_i\) \((y_i - \hat y_{(-i)})^2\): squared error on point \(i\) when it is left out \(\mathrm{CV}_{(n)}\) leave-one-out cross-validation estimate of the test MSE \(k\) number of folds in \(k\)-fold cross-validation (not the \(K\) of KNN) \(\mathrm{MSE}_j\) MSE on fold \(j\) for the model fitted without it \(\mathrm{CV}_{(k)}\) \(k\)-fold cross-validation estimate of the test MSE \(v_{50}\) vibration at which the fitted probability of a motor fault is 50% SE standard error: the “\(\pm\)” of an estimate A hyperparameter is a setting that we choose rather than fit from the data, such as the degree of a polynomial, the \(K\) of KNN or the step size of gradient descent. Choosing hyperparameters is the main use of cross-validation.
Example: calibrating a thermistor# An NTC thermistor: its resistance falls with temperature along a curve, not a line. Photo: Soumyapatra13, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) is a resistor whose resistance \(R\) falls steeply as it warms. Thermistors are cheap, sensitive temperature sensors used in appliances, cars and instruments. We have 40 readings of \(R\) (in k\(\Omega\)) against a reference thermometer, from 0 to 100 \(^\circ\)C; the resistance falls from about 33 k\(\Omega\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C to 0.7 k\(\Omega\) at 100 \(^\circ\)C.
The 40 thermistor readings: resistance (logarithmic scale) against temperature. The resistance is 10 kΩ at 25 °C and 0.7 kΩ at 100 °C. Physics (the “\(B\)-parameter equation”) says that \(1/T_K\) is linear in \(\ln R\):
\[ \frac{1}{T_K} = \frac{1}{298.15} + \frac{1}{B}\ln\frac{R}{10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}, \]where \(T_K\) is the temperature in kelvin and \(B = 3950\) K is a constant of the thermistor. So \(T\) is a smooth curve in \(\ln R\). We model it with a polynomial in \(x = \ln R\):
\[ T = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \dots + \beta_d x^d . \]This is still linear in the coefficients, so it is fitted by least squares (Lecture 2). Which degree \(d\)? Too low underfits; too high fits the noise. We need the test error of each degree, but have only 40 readings.
Worked numbers
Solving the \(B\)-equation for \(R\) at 100 \(^\circ\)C: \(R = 10\exp[3950(1/373.15 - 1/298.15)] = 10\exp(3950 \times (-0.000674)) = 10\exp(-2.662) = 0.70\) k\(\Omega\).
The validation-set approach# Two ways to keep data aside: one split, or leave out one point at a time. The simplest idea is to hold back part of the data and use it as a test set:
Split the data at random into two halves. Fit each candidate model on the training half. Measure its MSE on the other half, the validation set. Validation MSE against polynomial degree for ten different random splits of the same 40 readings. All agree that degree 1 is bad (MSE about 7), but they disagree about the rest. The approach has two problems:
The answer depends on the split. With only 20 validation points the estimate is noisy: the ten splits above chose degrees 5, 3, 2, 8, 4, 3, 9, 3, 2 and 3. Only half the data are used for fitting. A model fitted on 20 points is worse than one fitted on 40, so the validation error overestimates the error of the final model. Validation set or test set? The two words are easily confused. A validation set is used to make a choice (which degree), so it influences the final model. A test set only reports how good the final model is, and is never used to choose anything.
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)# Let each point take a turn as a one-point test set:
Leave out point 1. Fit the model on the other \(n - 1\) points. Predict point 1 and record its squared error \(\mathrm{MSE}_1 = (y_1 - \hat y_{(-1)})^2\). Repeat for every point \(i = 1, \dots, n\). The subscript \((-i)\) means “with point \(i\) removed”, so \(\hat y_{(-i)}\) is the prediction for point \(i\) from the model fitted without it. The LOOCV estimate of the test MSE is the average:
\[ \mathrm{CV}_{(n)} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{MSE}_i . \] Good: every fit uses almost all the data, and there is no randomness: LOOCV always gives the same answer. Bad: it needs \(n\) fits, which is slow for big data or slow models. (For least squares there is a shortcut that needs only one fit, ISLP equation 5.2, but not for most other methods.) \(k\)-fold cross-validation# 5-fold cross-validation: every point is used once to measure the error. A compromise between the validation set and LOOCV:
Split the data at random into \(k\) groups of about equal size, called folds. Leave out fold 1; fit on the other \(k - 1\) folds; compute the MSE on fold 1, \(\mathrm{MSE}_1\). Repeat for every fold \(j = 1, \dots, k\). The \(k\)-fold estimate is the average over the folds:
\[ \mathrm{CV}_{(k)} = \frac1k \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mathrm{MSE}_j . \]Every point is left out exactly once. The usual choice is \(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\); with \(k = 10\) and \(n = 40\), each fit uses 36 points and each fold tests 4. LOOCV is the special case \(k = n\). (Beware a clash of letters: ISLP uses \(K\) both for folds and for the neighbours of KNN.)
5-fold cross-validation: in each of the five rounds the red fold is left out and the blue folds are used for fitting. Example: the 5-fold cross-validation estimate# A thermistor model is fitted 5 times, each time leaving out one fold. The MSEs on the left-out folds are 0.41, 0.38, 0.52, 0.45 and 0.39 °C². What is the cross-validation estimate of the test MSE, and how many model fits did it cost? How many would LOOCV cost with \(n = 60\) readings?
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \mathrm{CV}_{(5)} = \frac{1}{5}(0.41 + 0.38 + 0.52 + 0.45 + 0.39) = 0.430\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}^2. \]It cost 5 fits. LOOCV leaves out one reading at a time: 60 fits (for least squares there is a shortcut formula, but not for most methods).
Thermistor: cross-validation picks the degree# Because the thermistor data are simulated, we can also compute the true test error on 5000 new readings, and check how well cross-validation estimated it.
Training MSE, LOOCV estimate, 10-fold CV estimate and true test MSE (from 5000 new readings) against the polynomial degree. Both CV estimates and the true test MSE are lowest at degree 3. The training MSE keeps falling, from 6.64 at degree 1 to 0.17 at degree 8: more flexibility always fits the training data better. (At degree 10 even the training MSE rises, to 0.93: \(x^{10}\) is so large that rounding errors spoil the least-squares solution.) LOOCV and 10-fold CV both pick \(d = 3\), with estimated MSE 0.254 and 0.253. The true test MSE is also lowest at \(d = 3\) (0.34). Cross-validation chose correctly. Its level differs a little (0.25 against 0.34) because 40 points give a noisy estimate, but the shape and the minimum agree. Cross-validation found the right model without a separate test set.
Worked numbers: the irreducible error
The reference thermometer's noise is 0.5 \(^\circ\)C, variance 0.25. The 1% noise on \(R\) adds about \((0.01 \times |dT/d\ln R|)^2\), with \(|dT/d\ln R| = T_K^2/B = 323^2/3950 = 26\) K at 50 \(^\circ\)C, i.e. \((0.26)^2 = 0.07\). The total, about 0.32, is close to the best test MSE of 0.34.
Try it. Change K. Each row is one fit; orange is the left-out fold. The CV error curve chooses the polynomial degree. Which \(k\)? And a warning# LOOCV or 10-fold? LOOCV has less bias (each fit uses \(n - 1\) points) but more variance: its \(n\) fits are almost identical, so their errors are highly correlated and do not average out. 10-fold CV needs 10 fits instead of \(n\) and is usually just as good; it is the standard choice (ISLP Section 5.1.4).
Classification: use the error rate in each fold instead of the MSE.
Do every step inside the folds. Every step that looks at the output \(Y\), such as choosing inputs, scaling or tuning, must be repeated inside each fold, using only that fold's training part. Otherwise the CV error is far too optimistic. The classic mistake (ESL Section 7.10.2): with 5000 random inputs and 50 samples, pick the 100 inputs most correlated with \(Y\), then cross-validate. CV reports near-zero error on pure noise, because the left-out folds had already been used to choose the inputs. In scikit-learn, a Pipeline keeps every step inside the folds.
The bootstrap# The bootstrap: resample the data with replacement, recompute the estimate many times, and look at the spread. How uncertain is a number that has no standard-error formula? Lecture 2 gave formulas for regression coefficients, but for most other quantities there is none. Ideally we would collect 1000 new data sets and see how much the number varies. We cannot, but we can imitate new data sets by resampling the one we have. This is the bootstrap:
Draw \(n\) rows with replacement from the \(n\) rows of the data. This is one bootstrap sample. Compute the number again from that sample. Repeat \(B\) times (typically \(B = 1000\)). The standard deviation of the \(B\) values is the standard error. “With replacement” means a drawn row is put back before the next draw, so some rows appear twice or more and some not at all. Each bootstrap sample is a plausible “other data set”.
Worked numbers
The probability that a given row is never drawn in \(n\) draws is \((1 - 1/n)^n\); for \(n = 200\) this is \(0.995^{200} = 0.367 \approx e^{-1}\). So about \(0.367 \times 200 \approx 73\) of 200 rows are missing from each bootstrap sample, and 63% are present.
Example: how many readings does a bootstrap sample miss?# A bootstrap sample draws \(n\) readings with replacement from \(n\). What is the probability that one given reading is never drawn, for \(n = 10\) and for \(n = 1000\)?
Solution triple-click to reveal One draw misses it with probability \(1 - 1/n\); \(n\) independent draws all miss it with probability \((1 - 1/n)^n\).
\(n = 10\): \(0.9^{10} = 0.349\) \(n = 1000\): \(0.999^{1000} = 0.368\), close to \(e^{-1} = 0.368\). So each bootstrap sample leaves out about a third of the readings (these are the “out-of-bag” readings used in Lecture 5).
Bootstrap example: the 50% vibration point# In Lecture 3 logistic regression gave the probability of a motor fault as \(\hat p(v) = \sigma(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 v)\). The vibration at which this probability is 50% is
\[ v_{50} = -\frac{\hat\beta_0}{\hat\beta_1} . \]It is a ratio of two estimates whose errors are correlated, so there is no simple standard-error formula. The bootstrap gives one: resample the 200 motors 1000 times, refit the logistic regression each time, and compute \(v_{50}\) each time.
Histogram of the 1000 bootstrap estimates of \(v_{50}\). Each bar counts the refits that gave a value in that range. The dashed line is the true value, 4.0 mm/s. Result: estimate 4.24 mm/s, bootstrap SE 0.14 mm/s, so \(v_{50} = 4.24 \pm 0.14\) mm/s. 95% interval: the 2.5% and 97.5% points of the 1000 values give \([3.96, 4.51]\), close to \(4.24 \pm 2 \times 0.14 = [3.96, 4.52]\). The true value, 4.0, lies inside. The same recipe works for almost any number computed from data: a median, a correlation, an AUC, a time constant.
Try it. Draw bootstrap samples. The histogram of the estimates is the uncertainty, without any formula.

title: Simple linear regression
content:
Simple linear regression# Linear regression is the simplest supervised method for predicting a number, and the foundation for much of what follows. This page fits a straight line to data by least squares, using the calibration of a temperature sensor as the running example, and then asks how far the result can be trusted: standard errors, \(t\)-statistics, \(p\)-values, and \(R^2\).
In the language of Lecture 1, linear regression is the simplest example of each ingredient:
Ingredient Linear regression Representation a straight line (or, with several inputs, a plane) Evaluation the sum of the squared errors Optimisation an exact formula, or gradient descent Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(X\), \(Y\) input and output in general \(i\), \(n\) data point number \(i = 1, 2, \dots, n\); \(n\) is the number of data points \(x_i\), \(y_i\) input and output of data point \(i\) \(\beta_0\) “beta nought” intercept: the value of \(Y\) when \(X = 0\) \(\beta_1\) “beta one” slope: the change in \(Y\) when \(X\) increases by 1 \(\varepsilon\) “epsilon” random error, average 0 \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\) “beta hat” the estimates of \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) computed from the data \(\hat y\), \(\hat y_i\) “y hat” predicted output for an input \(x\); for data point \(i\) \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\) “x bar”, “y bar” averages of the inputs and of the outputs \(\sum_i\) “sum over i” add up over all data points \(i = 1, \dots, n\) \(e_i\) residual of data point \(i\): \(y_i - \hat y_i\) RSS residual sum of squares, \(\sum_i e_i^2\) \(\sigma\) “sigma” standard deviation of the noise \(\varepsilon\) SE standard error: the standard deviation of an estimate over repeated experiments \(t\) \(t\)-statistic: an estimate divided by its standard error \(p\) \(p\)-value (see below); not to be confused with the number of inputs \(p\) RSE residual standard error, an estimate of \(\sigma\) TSS total sum of squares, \(\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2\) \(R^2\) “R squared” fraction of the variation in \(Y\) explained by the model \(V\), \(T\) sensor voltage (mV) and reference temperature (\(^\circ\)C) in the example Three marks on symbols: hat, bar and sum# Three marks appear in nearly every formula from now on.
Mark Meaning Example hat: \(\hat y\) predicted or estimated from data \(\hat y_i\) = the value our line predicts for data point \(i\) bar: \(\bar x\) the average \(\bar x = (x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n)/n\) sum: \(\sum_i\) add up over all data points \(\sum_i x_i = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n\) The hat is the most important mark of the course. \(y_i\) is what was measured; \(\hat y_i\) is what the model says. Their difference is the error the model makes on that point. A hat on a coefficient, \(\hat\beta_1\), means the value estimated from our data, as opposed to the unknown true value \(\beta_1\).
Example. For \(x_1 = 2\), \(x_2 = 4\), \(x_3 = 9\): \(\sum_i x_i = 2 + 4 + 9 = 15\) and \(\bar x = 15/3 = 5\). The deviations from the average are \(-3, -1, +4\), and they add up to zero. Deviations from the average always add up to zero, which is why the formulas below square them.
What is linear regression?# An LM35 temperature sensor: its output voltage rises in a straight line with temperature. Calibrating it is a linear regression. Photo: Nevit Dilmen (talk), Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 Linear regression assumes that the output \(Y\) changes in a straight line with the input \(X\): each extra unit of \(X\) changes \(Y\) by the same amount, wherever we are on the line. Real relationships are rarely exactly straight, but over a limited range many are close enough. A linear model is simple, fast and easy to interpret, and it often predicts well.
The model has a fixed form, chosen by us, and some numbers left open, the coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots\) (Greek “beta”; the subscript only counts them). Fitting the model means finding those numbers from the data.
“Linear” means linear in the coefficients, not that the graph is a straight line. The curve \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2\) is a parabola in \(X\), but it is still a sum of coefficients times known numbers (\(1\), \(X\), \(X^2\)), so the same method fits it. We use this on the next page.
As the statistician George Box put it, “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” No model captures reality exactly; the question is whether it is good enough for the purpose.
A straight line is a model; whether it is a good one is what this page is about. xkcd #1725 “Linear Regression” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. The model with one input# The simple linear regression model is
\[ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon , \]output = intercept + slope \(\times\) input + random error. Here \(\beta_0\), the intercept, is the value of \(Y\) when \(X = 0\); \(\beta_1\), the slope, is the change in \(Y\) for each unit increase of \(X\); and \(\varepsilon\) is everything the straight line does not capture (noise, unmeasured effects), with average zero. \(\varepsilon\) is not a mistake in the model but the scatter of real measurements: two readings at the same temperature never give exactly the same voltage.
The true coefficients are never known exactly. From \(n\) data points we compute estimates \(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\), and then predict the output for any input \(x\) as
\[ \hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x . \]Running example: calibrating a temperature sensor. Analogue temperature sensors such as the LM35 give an output voltage \(V\) that rises with temperature \(T\):
\[ V = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T . \]The slope \(\beta_1\) is the sensitivity in mV per \(^\circ\)C; the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the offset, the output at 0 \(^\circ\)C, in mV. We take \(n = 20\) readings, each pairing the sensor voltage with the true temperature from a trusted reference thermometer. The datasheet promises a sensitivity of 10 mV/\(^\circ\)C and no offset. Our job: measure both, with their uncertainties, and check the datasheet. Calibration is an everyday task in instrumentation, and it is a linear regression.
Least squares: what is the “best” line?# Least squares makes the total area of the squared residuals as small as possible. For each data point, the residual is measured minus predicted:
\[ e_i = y_i - \hat y_i . \]It is the vertical distance from the point to the line: positive if the point lies above the line, negative if below. Square each residual and add them up to get the residual sum of squares
\[ \mathrm{RSS} = e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \dots + e_n^2 = \sum_i \bigl(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\bigr)^2 . \]Squaring stops positive and negative residuals from cancelling (without it, a line far above some points and far below others could have residuals adding to zero), and it makes large residuals count heavily. The RSS is in the units of \(y\) squared, here mV\(^2\).
Least squares chooses, out of all possible straight lines, the one with the smallest RSS.
The 20 calibration readings (sensor voltage in mV against reference temperature in °C) and their least-squares line. The points lie very close to the line: the noise, about 15 mV, is small compared with the range of the output, 60 to 920 mV. Try it. Move the intercept and the slope. The red lines are the residuals; least squares makes the sum of their squares (the RSS) as small as possible. Then press Least squares. The least-squares line# The RSS is a function of the two unknowns \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). At its minimum both partial derivatives are zero. Solving those two equations gives
\[ \hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x . \]In words: the slope is how \(x\) and \(y\) vary together, divided by how much \(x\) varies. The numerator is large and positive when points with \(x\) above average also have \(y\) above average; the denominator measures the spread of \(x\). The second formula says that the least-squares line always passes through the point of averages \((\bar x, \bar y)\).
Derivation Write \(\mathrm{RSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\) and use the chain rule.
\(\partial\mathrm{RSS}/\partial\beta_0 = -2\sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i) = 0\) gives \(n\beta_0 = \sum_i y_i - \beta_1\sum_i x_i\), so \(\beta_0 = \bar y - \beta_1\bar x\).
\(\partial\mathrm{RSS}/\partial\beta_1 = -2\sum_i x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1x_i) = 0\). Substitute \(\beta_0\): \(\sum_i x_i\,[(y_i - \bar y) - \beta_1(x_i - \bar x)] = 0\). Since \(\sum_i \bar x (y_i - \bar y) = 0\) and \(\sum_i \bar x (x_i - \bar x) = 0\) (deviations from the average add to zero), \(x_i\) can be replaced by \(x_i - \bar x\), giving \(\beta_1 = \sum_i(x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) / \sum_i(x_i - \bar x)^2\).
Try it yourself before opening this box: it needs only the chain rule.
Calibration: the result# For the 20 readings, the averages are \(\bar T = 47.7\) \(^\circ\)C and \(\bar V = 471.6\) mV, and the least-squares line is
\[ \hat V = 2.5 + 9.83\,T . \] Worked numbers
From the data: \(\sum_i(T_i - \bar T)(V_i - \bar V) = 154\,992.3\) and \(\sum_i(T_i - \bar T)^2 = 15\,764.0\).
\(\hat\beta_1 = 154\,992.3 / 15\,764.0 = 9.832\) mV/\(^\circ\)C.
\(\hat\beta_0 = 471.64 - 9.832 \times 47.71 = 471.64 - 469.09 = 2.55 \approx 2.5\) mV (2.54 with unrounded averages).
Sensitivity: \(\hat\beta_1 = 9.83\) mV/\(^\circ\)C, close to the datasheet's 10. Is 9.83 consistent with 10? Offset: \(\hat\beta_0 = 2.5\) mV, where the datasheet says 0. Is 2.5 mV a real offset? Every estimate from noisy data differs a little from the truth, so neither question can be answered by looking at the numbers alone. The next three sections answer them.
Using the calibration. Suppose the sensor reads \(V = 500\) mV. Invert the line:
\[ T = \frac{V - \hat\beta_0}{\hat\beta_1} = \frac{500 - 2.54}{9.832} \approx 50.6\ ^\circ\mathrm C . \]With the datasheet formula (\(T = V/10\)) the answer would be 50.0 \(^\circ\)C; the calibration corrects it by 0.6 \(^\circ\)C. This is the purpose of a calibration: to turn a raw sensor reading into a reliable temperature.
Example: calibrating a pressure sensor# Five readings give the sensor voltage \(V\) (mV) at reference pressures \(P\) (kPa):
\(P\) 0 25 50 75 100 \(V\) 2.1 51.8 101.0 150.6 199.5 Find the least-squares line \(\hat V = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 P\), then the pressure for a reading of \(V = 120\) mV.
Solution triple-click to reveal Averages: \(\bar P = 50\) kPa, \(\bar V = 101.0\) mV.
\[ \sum_i (P_i - \bar P)(V_i - \bar V) = 12340, \qquad \sum_i (P_i - \bar P)^2 = 6250 \]so \(\hat\beta_1 = 12340/6250 = 1.9744\) mV/kPa and \(\hat\beta_0 = \bar V - \hat\beta_1\bar P = 101.0 - 1.9744 \times 50 = 2.28\) mV.
For \(V = 120\) mV: \(P = (120 - 2.28)/1.9744 = 59.6\) kPa.
How sure are we? The standard error# A standard error turns one estimate into a range: the true value is probably within ±2 SE. If we repeated the calibration with 20 new readings, the noise would be different, and so would the fitted slope. The standard error (SE) of the slope is the standard deviation of \(\hat\beta_1\) over many such repetitions. It is the “\(\pm\)” of the result. For simple linear regression
\[ \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}} , \]the noise divided by the spread of \(x\). Here \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the noise \(\varepsilon\). The slope is uncertain when the noise is large, and well determined when the \(x\) values are spread out. In practice \(\sigma\) is unknown and is replaced by its estimate from the data, the residual standard error (RSE), defined below.
A 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is
\[ \hat\beta_1 \pm 2\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1). \]An interval built this way contains the true value in about 95 of every 100 repetitions of the experiment. (The exact multiplier is 2.10 for 20 readings; 2 is the usual rounded value.) Note what “95%” means: it is a property of the method, over many repeats, not a probability attached to this one interval.
Calibration data. \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = 0.13\) mV/\(^\circ\)C, so \(\beta_1 = 9.83 \pm 0.13\) mV/\(^\circ\)C and the 95% interval is \([9.58,\ 10.09]\). The datasheet value, 10, lies inside: 9.83 is only \(0.17/0.13 = 1.3\) standard errors below 10. The measured sensitivity is consistent with the datasheet.
Worked numbers
\(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \mathrm{RSE}/\sqrt{15\,764.0} = 15.92/125.55 = 0.127\) mV/\(^\circ\)C.
Interval: \(9.832 - 2 \times 0.127 = 9.58\); \(9.832 + 2 \times 0.127 = 10.09\).
Three ways to make the SE smaller, and so the calibration more precise: less noise (a quieter sensor, or averaging), more data, and a wider range of \(x\) (readings spread over the whole working range).
The standard error of the intercept \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)^2 = \sigma^2\,\bigl[1/n + \bar x^2/\sum_i(x_i - \bar x)^2\bigr]\). Here \(15.92^2 \times (1/20 + 47.71^2/15\,764.0) = 253.4 \times (0.05 + 0.1444) = 49.3\), so \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0) = 7.0\) mV. The intercept is uncertain because all the data are far from \(T = 0\).
Is the effect real? The \(t\)-statistic# To test the idea “no effect”, i.e. that the true coefficient is exactly 0 (statistics books call this the null hypothesis), compute
\[ t = \frac{\text{estimate}}{\text{standard error}} = \frac{\hat\beta_1}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)} . \]\(t\) counts how many standard errors the estimate lies from zero. Write \(|t|\) for its size, ignoring the sign; a negative \(t\) is just as strong evidence as a positive one.
\(|t|\) large (more than about 2): an estimate this far from zero would be rare if the true value were zero, so the effect is real. Equivalently, the 95% interval does not contain 0. \(|t|\) small: the estimate could be zero plus noise. Calibration data. Sensitivity: \(t = 9.832/0.127 = 77.5\). Offset: \(t = 2.54/7.02 = 0.36\). The sensitivity is 77 standard errors from zero; the offset is less than one. These are the two possible outcomes: one clearly real, one indistinguishable from zero.
Example: the t-statistic of the sensitivity# The calibration gives the sensitivity \(\hat\beta_1 = 9.83\) mV/°C with standard error \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = 0.12\) mV/°C. (a) Test \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) (the null hypothesis that the sensor does not respond). (b) Is the datasheet value of 10 mV/°C consistent with the data?
Solution triple-click to reveal (a) \(t = \hat\beta_1/\mathrm{SE} = 9.83/0.12 = 81.9\). This is enormous (anything beyond about 2 is significant at 5%): the sensor certainly responds to temperature.
(b) Test against 10 instead of 0: \(t = (9.83 - 10)/0.12 = -1.42\). \(|t| < 2\), so the difference from the datasheet is within the noise. A 95% interval is \(9.83 \pm 2 \times 0.12 = [9.59, 10.07]\), which contains 10.
The \(p\)-value# The \(p\)-value answers: if there were no effect, how likely is it that noise alone would give a \(|t|\) at least this large? It is computed from the \(t\) distribution with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom, and statistical software reports it alongside every coefficient.
Small \(p\): noise alone rarely does this, so the effect is probably real. By convention, \(p < 0.05\) is called significant. This is a convention, not a law of nature. Careful: \(p\) is not the probability that the effect is zero. A large \(p\) means “no evidence of an effect”, not “no effect”. With only three readings almost nothing is significant, however real. The calibration results in the form software prints them:
estimate SE \(t\) \(p\) offset \(\hat\beta_0\) (mV) 2.5 7.0 0.36 0.72 sensitivity \(\hat\beta_1\) (mV/\(^\circ\)C) 9.83 0.13 77.5 \(\approx 0\) The sensitivity is certainly real (of course: the sensor responds to temperature). The offset is only 0.36 standard errors from zero: an offset of 2.5 mV is exactly what noise alone would often produce, so the data are consistent with the datasheet's zero offset. Conclusion: the sensor meets its datasheet within the uncertainty.
How not to read a p-value. xkcd #1478 “P-Values” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. How good is the fit? RSE and \(R^2\)# R² compares the spread left around the line (RSS) with the spread around the average (TSS). Two numbers summarise how well the line fits.
The residual standard error is the typical size of a residual:
\[ \mathrm{RSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n - 2}} . \]It estimates the noise \(\sigma\), in the units of \(y\). We divide by \(n - 2\) rather than \(n\) because two coefficients were estimated from the same data, which makes the residuals slightly smaller than the true errors.
The \(R^2\) statistic is the fraction of the variation in \(Y\) that the model explains:
\[ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}}, \qquad \mathrm{TSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2 . \]The total sum of squares TSS is the variation of \(y\) around its average before using \(x\); RSS is what is left after the fit; their ratio is the fraction left unexplained. \(R^2 = 0\) means the model explains nothing, \(R^2 = 1\) a perfect fit. \(R^2\) has no units, which makes it easy to compare between problems.
Calibration data. \(\mathrm{RSE} = 15.9\) mV, close to the true noise of 15 mV. Divided by the sensitivity, \(15.9/9.83 = 1.6\) \(^\circ\)C: a single reading of this sensor is uncertain by about \(\pm 1.6\) \(^\circ\)C. \(R^2 = 0.997\): temperature explains 99.7% of the variation in the output.
Worked numbers
\(\mathrm{RSS} = \mathrm{RSE}^2 \times (n - 2) = 15.92^2 \times 18 = 4562\) mV\(^2\). \(\mathrm{TSS} = 1\,528\,457\) mV\(^2\), so \(R^2 = 1 - 4562/1\,528\,457 = 1 - 0.0030 = 0.997\).
What counts as a “good” \(R^2\) depends on the field. A calibration expects more than 0.99; \(R^2 = 0.9\) would mean a faulty sensor. A model of household electricity use from survey data with \(R^2 = 0.5\) may be excellent, because people are unpredictable.
Example: RSE and R² from the sums# A fit to \(n = 20\) calibration readings has \(\mathrm{RSS} = 4480\) mV² and total sum of squares \(\mathrm{TSS} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2 = 1\,515\,000\) mV². Compute the residual standard error and \(R^2\).
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \mathrm{RSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n-2}} = \sqrt{\frac{4480}{18}} = 15.8\ \mathrm{mV}, \qquad R^2 = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{4480}{1\,515\,000} = 0.9970. \]A typical reading lies about 15.8 mV from the line, and the line explains 99.70% of the variation in the voltage.

title: The maximal margin classifier
content:
The maximal margin classifier# Trees cut the input space into boxes. Support vector machines take a different view of classification: look for the widest possible gap between the classes, and, if needed, bend that gap into a curve. This page covers the first step, for classes that a straight line can separate completely: hyperplanes, the margin, and support vectors.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning g/mL, mS/cm grams per millilitre (density); millisiemens per centimetre (electrical conductivity) \(X_1\), \(X_2\) the two inputs (standardised density and conductivity of a milk sample) \(p\) number of inputs \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) coefficients that set the position and tilt of the separating line \(f(x)\) \(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2\): its sign gives the class \(y_i\) class of point \(i\), coded \(+1\) or \(-1\) \(M\) the margin: distance from the line to the nearest point (half the width of the “street”) \(w\), \(b\) scikit-learn's names for the coefficients \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\) and the intercept \(\beta_0\) \(\lVert w\rVert\) “length of w” \(\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2}\) Example: has water been added to the milk?# Milk testing has a long history (a dairy-school laboratory, 1890s). Today an instrument and a classifier can do it. Photo: Unknown authorUnknown author, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain Adding water to milk changes two easily measured properties:
it lowers the density: water (1.000 g/mL) is lighter than milk (about 1.030 g/mL), so each 10% of added water lowers the density by about 0.003 g/mL; it lowers the electrical conductivity, because milk's conductivity comes from dissolved salts, and water dilutes them. Both are measured with cheap instruments: a lactometer (a float, calibrated for milk, that reads its density; used at collection centres) and a conductivity probe. The output is pure or adulterated.
We use two data sets:
A: 30 samples in which the watered samples have so much water added that the classes separate completely. Used on this page. B: 200 samples in which the classes overlap. Used on the next page. Both inputs are standardised (mean 0, standard deviation 1). Density varies by thousandths and conductivity by tenths; without standardising, every distance would be dominated by conductivity, and SVMs are built on distances.
A hyperplane# With two inputs, a hyperplane is a straight line:
\[ \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 = 0 . \]With \(p\) inputs it is a flat surface of dimension \(p - 1\): a line in two dimensions, an ordinary plane in three, and so on.
A hyperplane classifies by the sign of \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2\): points with \(f(x) > 0\) belong to one class, points with \(f(x) < 0\) to the other. The line divides the plane into two halves.
The size of \(f(x)\) tells the confidence: the farther a point is from the line, the surer we are of its class. If the coefficients are scaled so that \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1\), then \(f(x)\) is exactly the signed distance from the line.
