Rules with “and” are interactions, and their thresholds are sharp; both are hard for linear models and natural for trees.
A decision tree# A decision tree is a set of yes/no questions; it cuts the input space into boxes. A tree asks yes/no questions, one input at a time. Each question is a node; each end of the tree is a leaf, which gives the prediction. A classification leaf predicts the majority class of the training machines that reach it; a regression leaf predicts their average.
The (pruned) tree fitted to the 500 machines. Vibration above 4.5 mm/s: faulty. Otherwise, temperature at most 65.9 °C: healthy. Otherwise, current at most 10.5 A: healthy; above it: faulty. Read the tree from the top. A machine with vibration 3 mm/s, temperature 70 \(^\circ\)C and current 12 A goes left (vibration \(\le 4.5\)), then right (temperature \(> 65.9\)), then right (current \(> 10.5\)): faulty. A technician can follow this without a computer.
How a tree is grown# Trees are grown by recursive binary splitting:
Try every input and every possible cut point. Keep the split that makes the two resulting groups most pure (each group as close as possible to a single class). Repeat inside each group, until the groups are very small or pure. Searching all possible trees is impossible, so this procedure is greedy: it picks the best split now, not the best tree overall. It is fast and works well in practice.
For classification, purity is measured by the Gini index of a group,
\[ G = \sum_k \hat p_k\,(1 - \hat p_k), \]where \(\hat p_k\) is the fraction of the group in class \(k\). \(G = 0\) when every machine in the group is the same class; with two classes, \(G = 0.5\) when they are half and half. (Regression trees use the RSS instead.) The quality of a split is the size-weighted average of the two groups' \(G\) values; the best split lowers it most.
Worked numbers
A group with 30% faulty: \(G = 0.3 \times 0.7 + 0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.42\). After a split into a group with 5% faulty and one with 90% faulty: \(G = 2 \times 0.05 \times 0.95 = 0.095\) and \(G = 2 \times 0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.18\). Both are much purer.
Try it. Slide the cut along the vibration axis. The grey curve is the Gini gain of every possible cut; a tree chooses the highest point. Press Best cut. Example: choosing a split with the Gini index# A node holds 40 faulty and 60 healthy machines. Two candidate splits:
A (vibration > 3 mm/s): left 10 faulty / 50 healthy, right 30 faulty / 10 healthy. B (temperature > 60 °C): left 25 faulty / 35 healthy, right 15 faulty / 25 healthy. Using the Gini index \(G = 2p(1-p)\) (two classes, \(p\) = fraction faulty), which split does the tree choose?
Solution triple-click to reveal Parent: \(p = 0.4\), \(G = 2(0.4)(0.6) = 0.480\).
A: left \(G = 0.278\) (60 machines), right \(G = 0.375\) (40). Weighted: \(0.6 \times 0.278 + 0.4 \times 0.375 = 0.317\). Gain \(= 0.163\).
B: left \(G = 0.486\) (60), right \(G = 0.469\) (40). Weighted \(= 0.479\). Gain \(= 0.001\).
The tree takes A: it purifies the children far more.
Pruning: grow big, then cut back# A tree grown until its leaves are pure overfits. In our data 5% of the labels were flipped at random, and a deep tree grows extra leaves just to isolate those wrong labels. The remedy is to grow a big tree and then cut it back.
Cost-complexity pruning chooses the sub-tree that minimises
\[ \text{training error} + \alpha \times (\text{number of leaves}). \]Like the lasso penalty of Lecture 4, \(\alpha\) trades fit for simplicity; for each \(\alpha\) there is a best sub-tree of the full tree. \(\alpha\) is chosen by 10-fold cross-validation (in scikit-learn it is ccp_alpha).
leaves depth test error full tree 36 11 0.110 pruned (\(\alpha\) by CV) 4 3 0.098 The pruned tree, shown above, found the rules: “vibration above 4.5 mm/s” and “hot and high current” are exactly two of the rules used to simulate the faults, and its thresholds (4.5, 65.9, 10.5) are close to the true ones (4.5, 65, 11). A third rule (“old and noisy”) affects few machines and was pruned away.
Try it. Grow the tree one level at a time. The boxes follow the data more and more closely: watch the test error. Trees: good and bad# Good Bad easy to explain and draw less accurate than the best methods no scaling needed; inputs of mixed types high variance: a small change in the data can give a very different tree find interactions (“hot and high current”) by themselves boundaries are made of steps Trees use only the order of the values, so scaling does not matter, and categories can be split directly. Their weakness is variance: if the first split changes, everything below it changes. The fix is to grow many trees and combine them.
Trees, like every model, should not be trusted outside the range of their training data. xkcd #605 “Extrapolating” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Bagging# Bagging: many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, then a vote. Bagging (bootstrap aggregation):
Draw \(B\) bootstrap samples from the training data (Lecture 4). Grow a deep, unpruned tree on each. Predict by majority vote (the class predicted by most trees) for classification, or by the average for regression. Each deep tree has low bias and high variance. Averaging many of them keeps the low bias and cancels much of the variance. If \(B\) independent estimates each have variance \(\sigma^2\), their average has variance \(\sigma^2/B\). Trees grown on bootstrap samples of the same data are not independent, so the reduction is smaller (see random forests below).
Out-of-bag (OOB) error. Each bootstrap sample leaves out about a third of the rows (37%, i.e. \(e^{-1}\)). Predict each row using only the trees that did not see it, and you get a free estimate of the test error without cross-validation.
OOB error on these machines The random forest's OOB error is 0.058, but its test error on 5000 new machines is 0.081. OOB estimates, like CV estimates, are noisy with only 500 training rows; here it is optimistic.
Random forests# A random forest is bagging with one change: at each split, only a random subset of \(m\) inputs is considered, usually \(m \approx \sqrt p\). Here \(p = 6\), so \(m = 2\) (\(\sqrt 6 \approx 2.4\), rounded down).
Why? In bagging every tree splits first on the strongest input (vibration), so the trees look alike and make the same mistakes. The variance of an average of \(B\) trees whose predictions have correlation \(\rho\) is
\[ \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 \](ESL Section 15.2). With many trees the second term vanishes and only \(\rho\sigma^2\) remains, so lowering the correlation \(\rho\) between trees is what helps. Forcing variety in the splits does exactly that.
In Python: RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_features="sqrt"). Random forests rarely overfit as trees are added; more trees just cost time.
Example: how many inputs at each split?# The six-sensor machines have \(p = 6\) inputs. (a) A random forest for classification tries \(m \approx \sqrt p\) inputs at each split: how many? (b) Bagging is a random forest with which \(m\)? (c) Why does choosing fewer inputs per split help?
Solution triple-click to reveal (a) \(\sqrt 6 = 2.45\), so \(m = 2\) inputs at each split.
(b) Bagging uses all inputs at every split: \(m = p = 6\).
(c) If one input is very strong, every bagged tree splits on it first, so the trees look alike and their errors are correlated; averaging correlated trees reduces the variance little. Forcing different inputs makes the trees differ, and averaging then cancels more of the noise.
Boosting# Boosting: small trees added one after another, each correcting the previous ones. Boosting grows small trees one after another, each correcting the ensemble so far:
Fit a small tree to the data. Fit the next tree to what is still wrong, the residuals (measured minus predicted). Add it to the ensemble with a small weight \(\lambda\), the learning rate. Repeat. The model learns slowly, fixing its mistakes a little at a time. Unlike bagging, the trees are not independent (ISLP Algorithm 8.2; for classification the “residuals” are the gradients of the cross-entropy of Lecture 3). Note that ISLP reuses the letters \(\lambda\) and \(d\) here with new meanings.
Boosting has three settings, all chosen by cross-validation:
the number of trees \(B\) (unlike random forests, boosting can overfit if \(B\) is too large); the learning rate \(\lambda\), e.g. 0.05 (a smaller \(\lambda\) needs more trees); the depth \(d\) of each tree, e.g. 1 or 2 (depth 2 lets each tree capture interactions between two inputs). Machines: the result# All methods scored on the 5000 test machines. Because 5% of the labels are random, the best possible error is about 0.05.
Method test error AUC Logistic regression 0.152 0.845 Tree, full 0.110 0.856 Tree, pruned 0.098 0.856 Bagging (300 trees) 0.080 0.913 Random forest (300 trees) 0.081 0.919 Boosting (300 trees) 0.081 0.907 Logistic regression struggles: thresholds and “and” rules cannot be written as a weighted sum of the inputs. One tree is better; many trees are better still: from 0.098 (one pruned tree) to 0.08, about a fifth fewer errors. The three ensembles are about equal here. With only six inputs, the random forest's input sampling gives little advantage over bagging. How many trees? One tree has an error of 0.12–0.13; the error falls quickly over the first 10–25 trees, and after about 100 trees nothing changes.
Test error against the number of trees. Random forest: 0.135 with 1 tree, 0.084 with 25, 0.081 with 300. Bagging: 0.123, 0.078 and 0.080. Which inputs matter? Variable importance# A forest of 300 trees cannot be read like a single tree, but it can report how much each input was used. For every split in every tree, the reduction in the Gini index is credited to the input used; the totals, scaled to 100%, are the variable importances.
Random-forest variable importance (Gini reduction, % of total): vibration 57, temperature 13, current 9, acoustic noise 8, running hours 7, humidity 6. Vibration dominates: on its own it explains most faults, through the first rule. Humidity plays no part in the faults, yet scores 6%. This measure favours inputs with many possible cut points: deep trees also split on noise, and a continuous input offers many cut points. Permutation importance (shuffle one input and measure how much the test error rises) avoids this bias.
Things to watch# Splines at the ends: there are few data near the edges, and the curve can swing. Check the plot. A single tree is unstable: refit it on another sample and it can change completely. Do not over-interpret one tree. Importance is not causation, and some importance measures are biased. Check by dropping the input and re-running cross-validation. Boosting can overfit if it runs for too many trees; tune it by cross-validation. Scaling: trees need none, but splines and GAMs use the units of each input. Summary of Lecture 5# Splines fit smooth curves piece by piece; choose the number of knots by cross-validation. GAMs add up one shape per input and stay interpretable. Trees split the inputs with yes/no questions; prune them by cross-validation. Bagging, random forests and boosting combine many trees for much better accuracy. Variable importance shows which inputs a forest uses.

title: Course wrap-up
content:
Course wrap-up# A look back over the whole course, and a guide to choosing a method for a problem of your own.
The course at a glance# The whole course in one loop. Lecture Main idea Example used 1 Introduction training versus test error; bias–variance cooling cup, KNN on motors 2 Linear regression least squares; SE and \(t\); gradient descent sensor calibration, solar panel 3 Classification logistic regression; ROC; LDA, QDA motor faults 4 Resampling, regularisation cross-validation; bootstrap; lasso thermistor, electronic nose 5 Non-linear models, trees splines; random forests; boosting building demand, six-sensor machines 6 Support vector machines maximal margin; kernels milk adulteration, shaft orbit 7 Neural networks backpropagation; CNNs; RNNs thermal images, demand forecasting 8 Unsupervised learning PCA; \(k\)-means; hierarchical clustering pump station, electricity customers The thread through all eight lectures: fit on training data, judge on new data.
Choosing a method# What is your output?
A number: regression. A category: classification. None: PCA or clustering. What are your inputs?
A table of measured features: linear or logistic regression, the lasso, random forests, boosting. Images: a convolutional network. Sequences: an autoregressive model, a recurrent network. Always:
start with a simple baseline (guess the average, or the most common class; then a linear or logistic regression); compare methods by cross-validation; test once, at the end, on data never used for any choice; check that the result makes physical sense. Someone has to label the training data. xkcd #1897 “Self Driving” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. A checklist for your own project# When you apply these methods to a problem of your own, write up:
the problem, and why it matters; the data: source, size, inputs, output; the methods you compared, with a table of 10-fold cross-validation errors (and the baseline); your best model, and what it tells you about the problem; its limitations, and what you would do next. Summary of Lecture 8# Unsupervised learning finds structure without an output to predict. PCA summarises many correlated variables with a few components; the scree plot shows how many to keep. The PCA reconstruction error detects readings that break the normal pattern. \(k\)-means and hierarchical clustering find groups; scaling decides what “similar” means. Clusters are a starting point: check that they are stable and meaningful.

title: Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes
content:
Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes# Logistic regression models the probability of each class directly. This page takes another route: describe what each class looks like, then use Bayes' theorem to work out which class a new observation most probably belongs to. It covers linear and quadratic discriminant analysis and naive Bayes, compares all the classifiers met so far on the same test data, and extends classification to more than two classes.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(\Pr(A \mid B)\) “probability of A given B” probability of \(A\) when \(B\) is known to be true (conditional probability) \(k\), \(l\) class labels (here faulty or healthy) \(\pi_k\) “pi k” prior probability of class \(k\): how common the class is, before we look at \(X\) \(f_k(x)\) “f k of x” density of the inputs in class \(k\): high where class-\(k\) points are common \(\sum_l\) “sum over l” add over all classes \(l\); it makes the probabilities add up to 1 normal (Gaussian) the bell-shaped distribution, set by its mean and spread \(\mu_k\) “mu k” mean of the inputs in class \(k\): the centre of its cloud of points \(\Sigma\) “capital sigma” covariance matrix: the spread of each input and how the inputs vary together; it sets the size, shape and tilt of a cloud. Here \(\Sigma\) is not a sum \(\Sigma_k\) covariance matrix of class \(k\) alone \(p\) number of inputs \(f_{kj}(x_j)\) distribution of input \(j\) alone in class \(k\) \(K\) number of classes (not the \(K\) of \(K\)-nearest neighbours) \(z_k\) linear score of class \(k\) in multi-class logistic regression Probability words# The methods on this page are described in the language of probability.
Conditional probability \(\Pr(A \mid B)\): the probability of \(A\) given that \(B\) is true. For example \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid v = 6\ \text{mm/s})\) is, among machines vibrating at 6 mm/s, the fraction that are faulty. Prior \(\pi_k\): the probability of class \(k\) before we look at the inputs, i.e. how common the class is. If 30% of machines in a plant are faulty, the prior for “faulty” is 0.3. Density \(f_k(x)\): how the inputs are spread in class \(k\); it is high where class-\(k\) points are common. For one input, think of a smoothed histogram of the readings from that class. Normal (Gaussian) distribution: the bell-shaped distribution, fixed by its mean \(\mu\) (Greek “mu”), the centre, and its spread. Covariance \(\Sigma\): with several inputs, the spread of each input and how the inputs vary together. With two inputs it is a \(2 \times 2\) table, with the two variances on the diagonal and the covariance (which sets the correlation) off it. It fixes the size, shape and tilt of the elliptical cloud of points. Beware: the same Greek letter \(\Sigma\) also means “sum”; the context tells which. Another route: model each class# Generative classifiers model how each class is spread, then pick the class whose curve is higher. Logistic regression models \(\Pr(Y = k \mid X)\) directly. It is a discriminative method: it describes only the boundary between the classes.
A generative method instead describes each class fully: what healthy machines look like, what faulty ones look like, and how common each is. Bayes' theorem then turns this into the probability of each class for a given input \(x\):
\[ \Pr(Y = k \mid X = x) = \frac{\pi_k\, f_k(x)}{\sum_l \pi_l\, f_l(x)} . \]The numerator is “how common class \(k\) is” times “how typical \(x\) is of class \(k\)”; the denominator, a sum over all classes \(l\), makes the probabilities add up to 1. We then predict the class with the largest probability. This is exactly the Bayes classifier of Lecture 1, with its ingredients now estimated from data:
the prior \(\pi_k\) is estimated by the fraction of class \(k\) in the training data; the density \(f_k(x)\) is estimated by a model of how \(X\) is distributed in class \(k\). The methods below differ only in how they model \(f_k\).
Machines. Of the 400 training machines, 122 are faulty, so \(\hat\pi_{\text{faulty}} = 122/400 = 0.305\) and \(\hat\pi_{\text{healthy}} = 0.695\). Before looking at the sensors, a machine is faulty with probability 0.305.
Worked numbers: Bayes' theorem for one machine
Suppose for some reading \(x\) the densities are \(f_{\text{faulty}}(x) = 0.02\) and \(f_{\text{healthy}}(x) = 0.01\) (made-up numbers). Then \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid x) = 0.305 \times 0.02/(0.305 \times 0.02 + 0.695 \times 0.01) = 0.0061/0.01305 = 0.47\). Although the reading is twice as typical of faulty machines, the prior tips the decision to healthy.
Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)# LDA assumes that each class is a normal (Gaussian) cloud of points, with
its own mean \(\mu_k\) (the clouds may sit in different places), but the same covariance \(\Sigma\) for all classes (the clouds have the same size, shape and tilt). With equal covariances, the quadratic terms in \(x\) cancel when the two class densities are compared, and the boundary between the classes is a straight line (ESL Section 4.3).
Machines. The estimated class means are: healthy, \(v = 2.5\) mm/s and \(T = 50.0\) \(^\circ\)C; faulty, \(v = 4.7\) mm/s and \(T = 60.8\) \(^\circ\)C. (The true values in the simulation are 2.5, 50 and 4.5, 60.)
LDA or logistic regression? Both give a straight-line boundary. LDA is more stable when the classes are well separated or the data are few: when a line separates the classes perfectly, the logistic coefficients grow without limit, but LDA's do not. When the Gaussian assumption is badly wrong, logistic regression is the safer choice.
Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA)# QDA lets each class have its own covariance \(\Sigma_k\), so the clouds may have different sizes and tilts. The boundary then becomes a curve (a quadratic one, hence the name).
The price is more parameters to estimate, so QDA needs more data. With two inputs each covariance has three numbers (two spreads and a correlation); QDA estimates one set per class, LDA one set in total. With \(p\) inputs a covariance has \(p(p + 1)/2\) numbers, so with many inputs the difference is large.
In our machines, faulty machines vary much more than healthy ones: about twice the spread, with a strong correlation between vibration and temperature, while healthy ones have neither. QDA suits this.
Decision boundaries on the machine data: logistic regression (black, a straight line) and QDA (red, a curve that wraps around the compact cloud of healthy machines). Naive Bayes# Naive Bayes assumes that the inputs are independent within each class (knowing one input tells us nothing about another), so the class density is a product of one-dimensional densities:
\[ f_k(x) = f_{k1}(x_1) \times f_{k2}(x_2) \times \dots \times f_{kp}(x_p), \]where \(f_{kj}(x_j)\) describes how input \(j\) alone is spread in class \(k\). Instead of a joint distribution for all inputs we estimate one simple distribution per input per class, and multiply.
Only one-dimensional distributions are needed, so naive Bayes works with many inputs and little data. The independence assumption is usually false, and the method is “naive” because it ignores, for instance, that in faulty machines vibration and temperature rise together (their correlation of 0.8 is thrown away). Yet it often still classifies well: its probabilities may be poor, but the ranking of the classes is often right, which is all a classifier needs. It shines in problems like spam filtering, with thousands of inputs (words), each simple on its own.
Comparing classifiers on the test machines# All the classifiers met so far, fitted on the same 400 training machines and scored on the same 2000 test machines. The test error is \(1 -\) accuracy; KNN uses standardised inputs.
Method test error AUC Always say “healthy” 0.296 0.50 Logistic regression 0.113 0.890 LDA 0.118 0.889 QDA 0.110 0.906 Naive Bayes 0.116 0.885 KNN, \(K = 1\) 0.170 0.797 KNN, \(K = 15\) 0.112 0.885 The first row is the baseline: 593 of the 2000 machines are faulty, so always saying “healthy” is wrong \(593/2000 = 29.6\%\) of the time. Any useful method must beat it. All the good methods reach about 11% error. The overlap of the classes sets a floor that no method can beat. QDA is best, because the classes really have different shapes: its assumption matches how the data were made. KNN with \(K = 1\) overfits: training error 0 (each training machine is its own nearest neighbour), test error 0.17. No method wins everywhere. On another data set the order may be reversed. Always compare methods on the same test data. More than two classes# To decide the type of fault (imbalance, misalignment or bearing wear) we need \(K = 3\) classes. Multi-class logistic regression gives each class \(k\) its own linear score,
\[ z_k = \beta_{0k} + \beta_{1k}X_1 + \beta_{2k}X_2 + \dots , \]and the softmax function turns the \(K\) scores into probabilities:
\[ \Pr(Y = k \mid X) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{e^{z_1} + e^{z_2} + \dots + e^{z_K}} . \]The exponentials make every number positive; dividing by their sum makes them add up to 1. We predict the class with the largest probability. With \(K = 2\), softmax reduces to the sigmoid.
Example. Scores \(z = (2, 1, 0)\) give \(e^2 = 7.39\), \(e^1 = 2.72\), \(e^0 = 1\), with sum 11.11, so the probabilities are \(0.665\), \(0.245\) and \(0.090\).
LDA, QDA, naive Bayes and KNN handle \(K\) classes directly. Softmax is also the last layer of most neural-network classifiers (Lecture 7).
Things to watch# Rare classes. If 99% of machines are healthy, “always say healthy” is 99% accurate and useless. Look at recall and precision, not only accuracy. In real plants faults are rare, so this matters. Standardise for KNN. KNN's distances mix mm/s and \(^\circ\)C. Temperatures vary by about 7.6 \(^\circ\)C and vibrations by about 1.5 mm/s, so without scaling the distance is dominated by temperature. Standardising lowers the error of KNN (\(K = 15\)) from 0.120 to 0.112. Logistic regression and LDA are not affected by scaling. Curved boundaries. Use QDA, or add inputs such as \(x^2\) or \(x_1x_2\) to logistic regression, as in Lecture 2. Perfectly separated classes. If a line separates the classes perfectly, the likelihood keeps improving as the S-curve becomes a sharper step, so the logistic coefficients grow without limit. Regularisation (Lecture 4) fixes this. Judge on test data, never on the training data. Summary of Lecture 3# Logistic regression: \(p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots)\); the log-odds is linear; it is fitted by maximum likelihood (minimum cross-entropy). A threshold turns a probability into a decision; its choice trades missed faults against false alarms. Judge a classifier with the confusion matrix, recall, precision and the ROC curve, on test data. LDA, QDA and naive Bayes model each class, then use Bayes' theorem. Try several methods and compare them on the same test data.

title: Gradient descent
content:
Gradient descent# For linear regression the normal equations give the best coefficients directly. Most later models (logistic regression, neural networks) have no such formula; they are trained by gradient descent, which walks downhill on the error step by step. We learn it here, on linear regression, because the right answer is already known, so we can watch the method find it.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(\ell_i\) “ell i” loss of data point \(i\): how wrong the model is on that one point \(J(\boldsymbol\beta)\) “J of beta” cost: the average loss over all \(n\) points; it depends on the coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\) \(\alpha\) “alpha” step size, also called the learning rate; chosen by us \(\dfrac{dJ}{d\beta}\) “d J d beta” ordinary derivative: slope of \(J\) when there is one coefficient \(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_j}\) “partial J partial beta j” partial derivative: slope of \(J\) when only \(\beta_j\) changes \(\nabla J\) “grad J” gradient: the list of all partial derivatives \((\partial J/\partial\beta_0, \dots, \partial J/\partial\beta_p)\) \(\leftarrow\) “becomes” assignment: the new value on the right replaces the old one \(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\) the column of all \(n\) residuals \(x_i\) row \(i\) of \(\mathbf X\): the inputs of data point \(i\), with the 1 for the intercept \(z\) a standardised input (no units) \(s\) standard deviation of an input: the typical distance of its values from their average Loss and cost# Two words appear in every later lecture and in every software library, often used loosely.
The loss says how wrong the model is on one data point. For regression we use half the squared residual:
\[ \ell_i = \tfrac12\,\bigl(y_i - \hat y_i\bigr)^2 . \]The cost is the average loss over all \(n\) points, one number for the whole data set:
\[ J(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac1n \sum_i \ell_i = \frac{1}{2n} \sum_i \bigl(y_i - \hat y_i\bigr)^2 . \]The cost depends on the coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\): change \(\boldsymbol\beta\), the line moves, and \(J\) changes. Dividing by \(n\) keeps the numbers of similar size whatever the size of the data set; the \(\tfrac12\) only cancels the 2 that appears when we differentiate.
Training a model means finding the \(\boldsymbol\beta\) with the smallest cost. This is true of every model in the course; only the form of the loss changes (Lecture 3 uses a different loss for classification).
Since \(J = \mathrm{RSS}/2n\) and dividing by a fixed number does not move the minimum, the best line is the same as the least-squares line. (Many books and libraries say “loss” for both meanings; in these notes loss is for one point and cost for the average.)
Example. Three points with residuals \(1, -2, 3\) have losses \(\tfrac12 \times 1^2 = 0.5\), \(\tfrac12 \times (-2)^2 = 2\) and \(\tfrac12 \times 3^2 = 4.5\), so the cost is \(J = (0.5 + 2 + 4.5)/3 = 2.33\). Check: \(\mathrm{RSS} = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14\) and \(\mathrm{RSS}/2n = 14/6 = 2.33\).
Walk downhill# Gradient descent walks downhill on the cost. The step size decides whether it crawls, runs, or flies off. The algorithm:
Start with any \(\boldsymbol\beta\) (for example all zeros). Repeat: \[ \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{new}} = \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{old}} - \alpha\,\nabla J . \] Stop when the cost \(J\) no longer falls. The gradient \(\nabla J\) points uphill, in the direction in which the cost rises fastest; a step against it goes downhill. The step size \(\alpha\) sets how far each step goes. Because the step is \(\alpha\) times the slope, steps shrink automatically as the slope flattens near the minimum: big steps where the cost is steep, small steps near the bottom.
\(\alpha\) is our first example of a hyperparameter: a setting that we choose, rather than one that is fitted from the data (Lecture 4 says more).
What is the gradient?# With one coefficient, \(\nabla J\) is just the ordinary derivative \(dJ/d\beta\), the slope of the cost curve.
If the slope is negative, the cost falls to the right, so we should increase \(\beta\). If the slope is positive, we should decrease \(\beta\). The minus sign in the update does exactly this: \(-\alpha \times (\text{negative slope})\) is a step to the right, towards the minimum.
With many coefficients, the gradient is a list of slopes, one per coefficient:
\[ \nabla J = \left(\frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_0}, \frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_p}\right). \]Each partial derivative \(\partial J/\partial\beta_j\) is the slope of \(J\) when only \(\beta_j\) changes and the others are held fixed. Together they point in the steepest uphill direction.
Gradient descent on the bowl-shaped cost \(J = (\beta - 2)^2\) with \(\alpha = 0.2\), starting at \(\beta = 0\). The red points are the successive steps, 0, 0.8, 1.28, 1.57, …, closing in on the minimum at \(\beta = 2\). Worked example. Take \(J = (\beta - 2)^2\), whose minimum is at \(\beta = 2\), with \(\alpha = 0.2\). The slope is \(dJ/d\beta = 2(\beta - 2)\).
Start at \(\beta = 0\): slope \(-4\), so \(\beta_{\text{new}} = 0 - 0.2 \times (-4) = 0.8\). At \(\beta = 0.8\): slope \(2(0.8 - 2) = -2.4\), so \(\beta = 0.8 + 0.2 \times 2.4 = 1.28\). At \(\beta = 1.28\): slope \(-1.44\), so \(\beta = 1.568\), and so on towards 2. Each step removes 40% of the remaining distance to 2, because \(\beta - 2\) is multiplied by \(1 - 2\alpha = 0.6\).
Gradient descent for linear regression# For the cost \(J(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) of linear regression, the gradient is \(\nabla J = -\frac1n\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)\), where \(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\) is the column of residuals. There are two common versions of the update.
Batch gradient descent uses all data points in each step:
\[ \boldsymbol\beta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\beta + \frac{\alpha}{n}\,\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\bigl(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\bigr). \]Stochastic gradient descent uses one data point \(i\) in each step, cycling through the data:
\[ \boldsymbol\beta \leftarrow \boldsymbol\beta + \alpha\,\bigl(y_i - \hat y_i\bigr)\,x_i . \]Each stochastic step is cheap, which is why this version is used for very large data sets and for neural networks. The arrow \(\leftarrow\) means “becomes”, as in a program: compute the right-hand side, then store it in \(\boldsymbol\beta\).
Reading the update. The step is proportional to the error \(y_i - \hat y_i\): a big mistake gives a big correction, a small mistake a small one. When a prediction is too low, the coefficients move so as to raise it, in proportion to the input values.
Good news for linear regression: the cost is a quadratic function of \(\boldsymbol\beta\), a single bowl with only one minimum (it is convex). Walking downhill always leads to the one best answer. Neural networks do not have this property.
Example: one step of gradient descent by hand# Fit \(y = \beta x\) (no intercept) to the points \((1, 2.2), (2, 3.9), (3, 6.1)\) with cost \(J(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \beta x_i)^2\). Start at \(\beta = 1\) with step size \(\alpha = 0.05\). Do one gradient-descent step. What is the exact minimiser?
Solution triple-click to reveal \[ \frac{dJ}{d\beta} = -\frac{2}{n}\sum_i x_i (y_i - \beta x_i) = -\frac{2}{3}\big[1(1.2) + 2(1.9) + 3(3.1)\big] = -9.533 \]Update: \(\beta \leftarrow 1 - 0.05 \times (-9.533) = 1.4767\).
Exact minimiser (set the derivative to zero): \(\beta = \sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2 = 28.3/14 = 2.0214\). One step moved from 1 to 1.4767, towards 2.0214.
Choosing the step size \(\alpha\)# We run gradient descent on the temperature-sensor calibration data of simple linear regression (with the temperature standardised, as explained in the next section), starting from \(\boldsymbol\beta = 0\), where the cost is \(1.49 \times 10^5\) mV\(^2\).
Cost against step number (40 steps, logarithmic vertical axis) for three step sizes on the calibration data: \(\alpha = 0.01\) (grey, too small), \(\alpha = 0.5\) (green, about right) and \(\alpha = 2.1\) (red, too large). Too small (\(\alpha = 0.01\)): very slow. After 40 steps the cost has only fallen to \(6.7 \times 10^4\) mV\(^2\). About right (\(\alpha = 0.5\)): the cost reaches its minimum, 114 mV\(^2\), by step 10, and the coefficients equal the least-squares values (9.832 mV/\(^\circ\)C and 2.54 mV). Too large (\(\alpha = 2.1\)): each step jumps past the minimum to a higher point on the other side, and the cost grows without limit. Always plot the cost at every step. It must go down. This is the simplest check that both the code and the step size are right.
Worked numbers
Minimum cost \(= \mathrm{RSS}/(2n) = 4562/40 = 114\) mV\(^2\). Cost at steps 0, 1, 2, 3 with \(\alpha = 0.5\): 149 435; 37 444; 9 447; 2 447 mV\(^2\), about four times smaller each step. With a standardised input, \(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X/n\) is the identity matrix, so \(\alpha = 1\) would reach the minimum in one step, and any \(\alpha > 2\) diverges.
Try it. Try \(\alpha = 0.1\), then \(0.9\), then \(1.05\). Small steps are slow, steps near 1 zig-zag, and steps above 1 diverge. Scale the inputs first# With the raw temperatures (6 to 93 \(^\circ\)C) only tiny steps are possible: even after 5000 steps the offset is still wrong (1.4 mV instead of 2.5 mV). The reason is the shape of the cost. With raw inputs the cost bowl is a long, narrow valley: very steep in the slope direction (temperatures are large numbers) and very flat in the intercept direction. A step size small enough not to blow up across the valley (at most \(6.5 \times 10^{-4}\) here) is far too small to make progress along it.
The cure is to standardise each input: subtract its average and divide by its standard deviation \(s\),
\[ z = \frac{x - \bar x}{s} . \]Every standardised input has average 0 and spread 1, so all directions of the bowl become equally steep, and about 10 steps are enough.
Rules.
Standardise the inputs before gradient descent. Compute \(\bar x\) and \(s\) from the training data only, and scale the test data with those same numbers, so that no information about the test data leaks into training. Sensor inputs often differ by many orders of magnitude (W/m\(^2\), \(^\circ\)C, mV, kHz), so scaling is a routine first step. In the solar data, \(G\) is in hundreds and \(T\) in tens; in a vibration data set, frequencies may be in kHz.
Worked numbers
For the calibration temperatures \(s = 28.1\) \(^\circ\)C. After fitting on \(z\), convert back: slope per \(^\circ\)C \(= \beta_z/s = 276.03/28.075 = 9.832\) mV/\(^\circ\)C; offset \(= \beta_{0z} - 9.832 \times 47.71 = 471.64 - 469.10 = 2.54\) mV, the least-squares values.
Summary of Lecture 2# Least squares chooses the line with the smallest residual sum of squares. Standard errors, \(t\) and \(p\) say how much to trust each coefficient; RSE and \(R^2\) say how well the model fits. With many inputs, \(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y\). Each coefficient holds the other inputs fixed. Categories enter as dummy variables; products of inputs give interactions; logarithms can straighten curves. Gradient descent finds the same answer step by step: standardise the inputs first, and watch the cost fall.

title: Kernels
content:
Kernels# Some boundaries are not straight. This page shows how a support vector classifier can draw curved boundaries by working, implicitly, with extra inputs: the kernel trick. A support vector classifier with a kernel is called a support vector machine (SVM).
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(x\), \(y\) the two probe readings: shaft position in two perpendicular directions (\(\mu\)m) \(\mu\)m “micrometre” a thousandth of a millimetre \(r\) distance of the shaft from the centre, \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) (\(\mu\)m) feature space the set of all inputs (features) the model uses \(x_i\), \(x_{ij}\) training point \(i\); input \(j\) of point \(i\) \(\sum_j\) add over the inputs \(j\) \(K(x_i, x_k)\) “kernel of x i and x k” a similarity between points \(i\) and \(k\) (not the \(K\) of KNN) \(d\) degree of the polynomial kernel \(\gamma\) “gamma” width parameter of the radial kernel: how fast the similarity falls with distance \(\exp(a)\) \(e^a\) \(C\) cost parameter (scikit-learn convention: small \(C\) = wide street) Example: a shaft orbit# Two probes record the shaft position; the orbit's shape tells healthy from misaligned. Large turbines, compressors and pumps carry two proximity probes at right angles. These eddy-current sensors measure the gap to the rotating shaft without touching it, giving the shaft's position \(x\), \(y\) in \(\mu\)m. Plotting \(y\) against \(x\) traces the shaft's orbit.
A healthy shaft stays near the centre. With unbalance (mass off-centre) or a rub (the shaft touching a fixed part), it swings far out, in any direction. The direction depends on the moment of the reading; only the distance from the centre matters. Our data: 300 training readings and 3000 test readings, 40% of them faults.
The training readings: healthy readings cluster near the centre; fault readings lie further out, in every direction. No straight line can do this# The kernel trick: in a bigger space the classes become separable by a straight line. The boundary should be a circle: faults lie outside it, healthy readings inside. Any straight line cuts the circle in half, so every linear classifier fails.
The remedy is the trick of Lecture 2: add new inputs, such as \(x^2\) and \(y^2\). With the new inputs \(u = x^2\) and \(v = y^2\), the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) becomes the straight line \(u + v = r^2\). In general, enlarge the feature space: a linear boundary in the enlarged space is a curved boundary in the original space.
Kernels# Adding many new inputs can be expensive. Fortunately, the support vector classifier never needs the inputs themselves: its solution can be written using only the inner products \(\sum_j x_{ij}x_{kj}\) between pairs of training points (ISLP Section 9.3.2), a measure of how similar two points are. A kernel \(K(x_i, x_k)\) replaces this inner product with another similarity. Doing so is equivalent to working in an enlarged feature space (possibly an infinite-dimensional one) without ever computing it. This is the kernel trick.
kernel \(K(x_i, x_k)\) what it does linear \(\sum_j x_{ij}x_{kj}\) the ordinary inner product: the support vector classifier polynomial \(\bigl(1 + \sum_j x_{ij}x_{kj}\bigr)^d\) equivalent to adding all products of inputs up to degree \(d\); with \(d = 2\): \(x_1^2\), \(x_2^2\), \(x_1x_2\) radial \(\exp\bigl(-\gamma \sum_j (x_{ij} - x_{kj})^2\bigr)\) depends only on the distance between the two points The radial kernel gives a similarity between 0 and 1: close to 1 for nearby points and close to 0 for distant ones. The parameter \(\gamma\) sets how fast it falls with distance; a large \(\gamma\) makes the kernel very local and the boundary wiggly.
Worked numbers
Radial kernel with \(\gamma = 0.1\), in standardised units: points at distance 1 have similarity \(e^{-0.1} = 0.90\); at distance 3, \(e^{-0.9} = 0.41\); at distance 5, \(e^{-2.5} = 0.08\).
Example: three kernels for the same pair of points# Compute \(K(\mathbf x, \mathbf x')\) for \(\mathbf x = (1, 2)\) and \(\mathbf x' = (2, 0)\) with the linear kernel \(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf x'\), the polynomial kernel \((1 + \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf x')^2\) and the radial kernel \(\exp(-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'\|^2)\) with \(\gamma = 0.5\).
Solution triple-click to reveal Linear: \(1 \times 2 + 2 \times 0 = 2\). Polynomial: \((1 + 2)^2 = 9\). Radial: \(\|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'\|^2 = (1-2)^2 + (2-0)^2 = 5\), so \(K = e^{-0.5 \times 5} = 0.082\). The radial kernel is a similarity between 0 and 1: near 1 for close points, near 0 for distant ones.
Shaft orbit: the result# \(C\) and \(\gamma\) were chosen together by 10-fold cross-validation over a grid of 20 combinations, \(C \in \{0.1, 1, 10, 100\}\) and \(\gamma \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5\}\). For the radial SVM this gave \(C = 10\), \(\gamma = 0.1\).
Method test error Logistic regression 0.375 Linear SVM 0.403 Polynomial SVM, \(d = 2\) 0.056 Radial SVM 0.060 Best possible (rule on the radius) 0.055 The radial SVM's decision boundary (black): a near-circle around the healthy readings, with mean radius 33.5 µm. Linear methods are no better than guessing. Always guessing “healthy” is wrong for the 40% of readings that are faults; logistic regression (0.375) and the linear SVM (0.403) do no better. Both kernels find a near-circle. The best possible rule, “fault if the distance from the centre exceeds 32.6 \(\mu\)m”, has error 0.055, and the SVMs are almost there. No rule can reach zero error, because the classes overlap in radius (healthy readings reach about 35 \(\mu\)m, faults come down to about 25 \(\mu\)m). The radial SVM uses 68 of the 300 readings as support vectors. If you know the physics, compute the right feature yourself. Here that is the radius \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). Logistic regression on \(r\) alone has test error 0.057, as good as the SVMs. Kernels help most when you do not know the right features.
Overfitting with a large \(\gamma\) \(\gamma = 5\) with \(C = 100\) gives a training error of 0.013 but a test error of 0.126. A very local kernel combined with expensive violations wraps the boundary around individual points.

title: Recurrent networks
content:
Recurrent networks# A convolutional network shares weights across space. A recurrent neural network (RNN) shares them across time: it reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a memory forward. This page explains the idea and uses it to forecast a building's electricity demand.
Notation on this page
Symbol Meaning \(t\) time step (here, hour) \(x_t\) input at time step \(t\) (e.g. the demand in hour \(t\)) \(h_t\) hidden state at time \(t\): the network's memory \(W\), \(U\), \(b\) weights applied to the previous hidden state, weights applied to the new input, and a bias \(g\) activation function GRU, LSTM gated recurrent unit; long short-term memory: recurrent units with “gates” that remember over longer spans AR(1), AR(24) autoregressive models: the next value is a linear function of the last 1 (or 24) values plus noise kW\(^2\) unit of the test MSE (squared error of a demand in kW) Sequences and memory# A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward. A recurrent network reads a sequence \(x_1, x_2, \dots\) one step at a time. Its hidden state \(h_t\) carries a memory of what came before, and is updated at every step:
\[ h_t = g\bigl(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b\bigr). \]The new memory depends on the old memory \(h_{t-1}\) and on the new input \(x_t\) (ISLP Section 10.5). The same weights \(W\), \(U\) and bias \(b\) are used at every step: the weights are shared along time, as a CNN shares them across space. The forecast is computed from the last hidden state.
An RNN reading the inputs \(x_{t-3}, \dots, x_t\): the hidden states are connected in a chain, and the forecast is made from the last one. Plain RNNs forget quickly. GRU and LSTM units add “gates”, small learned switches that decide what to keep in the memory and what to forget, so they can remember over longer spans.
Example: forecasting a building's demand# The office building of Lecture 5 is metered every hour for 200 days. The task: from the last 24 hours of demand, forecast the next hour.
The demand follows the daily pattern, the weather, and disturbances that last a few hours: each hour's disturbance keeps 70% of the previous hour's, plus new random noise (an AR(1) process, short for autoregressive of order 1).
Split by time. Train on the first 150 days and test on the last 50 days (\(50 \times 24 = 1200\) forecasts). For forecasting, never split at random: a random split lets the model see the hours just after the ones it predicts, which is impossible in real use. Train on the past, test on the future.
Forecasting: the result# Method test MSE (kW\(^2\)) Same hour yesterday 45.8 Linear model on the last 24 hours, AR(24) 13.7 Recurrent network (GRU, 929 parameters) 11.6 Noise floor (unpredictable part) 9.0 The first 4 test days: actual demand with the AR(24) and GRU forecasts. Both follow the daily pattern closely; the GRU follows the disturbances a little better. The naive forecast (“same hour yesterday”) ignores the current disturbance. The AR(24) model, a linear regression on the last 24 values (Lecture 2), uses it and does far better. The GRU does somewhat better still. No model can beat 9.0 kW\(^2\): the new noise each hour is unpredictable. ISLP reaches a similar conclusion on stock-market data: recurrent networks help only modestly over a good linear autoregressive model.
Worked numbers
GRU with 16 hidden units and 1 input: \(3 \times (16 \times 1 + 16 \times 16 + 16 + 16) = 3 \times 304 = 912\) parameters (three gates, each with input weights, recurrent weights and two bias vectors), plus the output \(16 + 1 = 17\): 929.

title: Statistical learning
content:
Statistical learning# This page sets up the mathematical picture behind every method in the course: an output that depends on some inputs through an unknown function, plus random noise. Learning means estimating that function from data. We first recall two words from statistics, the expected value and the variance, because the rest of the course uses them constantly.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(Z\); \(z_1, z_2, \dots\) a random quantity (it changes each time we measure it); its measured values \(\mathbb E(Z)\) “expected value of Z” the average of \(Z\) over very many repeats \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\) “variance of Z” the average squared distance of \(Z\) from its average \(\sigma\) “sigma” standard deviation \(= \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}\): the typical size of the spread \(X = (X_1, \dots, X_p)\) the inputs in general; \(X_j\) is the \(j\)-th input \(Y\) the output in general \(f\) the true relation between inputs and output: fixed, but unknown \(\varepsilon\) “epsilon” random error (noise): average zero, unrelated to \(X\) \(\hat f\), \(\hat Y\) “f hat”, “Y hat” our estimate of \(f\), and its prediction \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\) \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\) “beta nought, beta one, …” parameters of a model Expected value and variance# A random quantity \(Z\) takes a different value each time it is measured, like the reading of a noisy thermometer. We write its measured values as \(z_1, z_2, \dots\).
The expected value \(\mathbb E(Z)\) is the average we would get if we measured \(Z\) very many times:
\[ \mathbb E(Z) \approx \frac{z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_m}{m} \qquad \text{for a large number of repeats } m . \](The sign \(\approx\) is there because a finite number of repeats only gets close to the long-run average.)
The variance measures the spread about that average. Take each value's distance from the average, square it, and average the squares:
\[ \operatorname{Var}(Z) = \mathbb E\bigl(Z - \mathbb E(Z)\bigr)^2 . \]A large variance means the values scatter widely. The variance is in squared units (for temperatures, \(^\circ\)C\(^2\)), so we often use its square root, the standard deviation
\[ \sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}, \]which is back in the units of \(Z\) and gives the typical size of the scatter.
Example. A thermometer with random noise of standard deviation \(\sigma = 2\) \(^\circ\)C measures a cup at 50 \(^\circ\)C. It reads 49.1, 51.8, 50.6, … The readings average to \(\mathbb E(Z) = 50\) \(^\circ\)C and their variance is \(\sigma^2 = 2^2 = 4\) \(^\circ\)C\(^2\).
Example: average and variance of mains voltage# Five readings of the mains voltage are 229.0, 231.5, 228.2, 232.1 and 230.2 V. Find the average, the variance (divide by \(n\)) and the standard deviation.
Solution triple-click to reveal Average: \(\bar v = (229.0 + 231.5 + 228.2 + 232.1 + 230.2)/5 = 230.20\) V.
Deviations from the average: -1.20, +1.30, -2.00, +1.90, +0.00. Squared: 1.4400, 1.6900, 4.0000, 3.6100, 0.0000.
Variance \(= (1.4400 + 1.6900 + 4.0000 + 3.6100 + 0.0000)/5 = 2.1480\) V², standard deviation \(= \sqrt{2.1480} = 1.466\) V.
The central equation: \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\)# Suppose we measure \(p\) inputs \(X = (X_1, X_2, \dots, X_p)\) and one output \(Y\). We assume
\[ Y = f(X) + \varepsilon . \] \(f\) is the true relation between the inputs and the output. It exists in nature, but we do not know it. \(\varepsilon\) (epsilon) is the random error: measurement noise and the effect of everything we did not measure. We assume it has average zero, \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon) = 0\) (it is as likely to push \(Y\) up as down), and that it is unrelated to \(X\), so it cannot be predicted from the inputs. Learning means finding an estimate \(\hat f\) of \(f\) from data, and then predicting \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\) for new inputs. The hat means “estimated from data”; \(\hat f\) is our model.
Capital letters \(X\), \(Y\) denote the quantities in general; small letters \(x_i\), \(y_i\) denote one measured observation. So \(Y\) is “panel power” in general, while \(y_3 = 78.5\) W is the power in reading 3.
Example: the solar panel. \(X_1\) is the irradiance, \(X_2\) the cell temperature and \(Y\) the power. Dust on the glass and wind cooling the panel also change the power, but we did not measure them, so their effect is part of \(\varepsilon\). No model built from \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) can predict it.
Reducible and irreducible error# How well can we predict? Measure it by the average squared prediction error over many new observations, \(\mathbb E(Y - \hat Y)^2\): the average of (measured \(-\) predicted)\(^2\). For a fixed input \(X\) it splits into two parts:
\[ \mathbb E\bigl(Y - \hat Y\bigr)^2 = \underbrace{\bigl[f(X) - \hat f(X)\bigr]^2}_{\text{reducible}} + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}} . \] The reducible error \([f - \hat f]^2\) arises because our estimate \(\hat f\) is not the true \(f\). A better method or more data can make it smaller. The irreducible error \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\) is the variance of the noise itself. No method can remove it, because the noise cannot be predicted from \(X\). The key consequence: even a perfect model, \(\hat f = f\), has average squared error \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\). Put \(\hat f = f\) in the equation and only the noise term remains. The noise sets a floor that no model can go below; we will see this floor in real numbers on the next page.
Where the equation comes from With \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) and \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\) for a fixed \(X\), expand the square:
\[ \mathbb E(Y - \hat Y)^2 = \mathbb E(f - \hat f + \varepsilon)^2 = (f - \hat f)^2 + 2(f - \hat f)\,\mathbb E(\varepsilon) + \mathbb E(\varepsilon^2). \]The middle term is zero because \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon) = 0\), and \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon^2) = \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) because \(\varepsilon\) has average zero.
Why estimate \(f\)? Prediction and inference# There are two reasons for estimating \(f\), and they lead to different choices of model.
Prediction. We want accurate predictions \(\hat Y\), and how \(\hat f\) works inside does not matter. It may be a black box, a model whose inner workings we never look at. Example: forecast tomorrow's panel output for the grid operator. Inference. We want to understand how \(Y\) depends on each input \(X_j\). Then \(\hat f\) must be simple enough to read. Example: solar cells lose efficiency as they heat up; how many watts are lost per degree? A simple model gives the answer as a single parameter (Lecture 2). Parametric and non-parametric methods# A parametric method fixes the form of f and learns a few numbers; a non-parametric method lets the data decide the shape. There are two broad ways to estimate \(f\).
Parametric methods work in two steps.
Assume a form for \(f\) with a fixed number of unknown parameters. The most common is the linear form \[ f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_p X_p . \] Here \(\beta_0\) (“beta nought”) is the value of \(f\) when all inputs are zero, and \(\beta_j\) is how much \(f\) changes when \(X_j\) increases by one unit with the other inputs held fixed. Fit the model: estimate the parameters \(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_p\) from the data. Learning \(f\) thus becomes learning \(p + 1\) numbers. That needs little data, and the numbers are easy to interpret. The weakness: if the assumed form is wrong (nature is not linear), no choice of the \(\beta\)'s can repair it, and the fit is poor.
Non-parametric methods assume no fixed formula for \(f\); they follow the data as closely as is reasonable. Examples are \(K\)-nearest neighbours (Classification) and decision trees (Lecture 5). They can fit many shapes of \(f\), but they need many more observations, they are harder to interpret, and they can end up following the noise (overfitting, explained on the next page).
Physics often supplies the form# Physics often tells us the form of f, for example exponential decay or Newton's law of cooling. Machine learning then only has to find the numbers. In physics we frequently know the formula and only need its constants. Newton's law of cooling says that a hot object cools towards the temperature of its surroundings as
\[ T(t) = T_{\mathrm{env}} + \bigl(T_0 - T_{\mathrm{env}}\bigr)\, e^{-kt}, \]where
\(T(t)\) is the temperature (\(^\circ\)C) at time \(t\) (minutes since the start), \(T_{\mathrm{env}}\) is the temperature of the surroundings, \(T_0\) is the temperature at \(t = 0\), \(k\) is the cooling rate (per minute): a larger \(k\) means faster cooling, \(e^{-kt}\) is an exponential decay that falls from 1 at \(t = 0\) towards 0. Check the two ends: at \(t = 0\), \(e^{0} = 1\) and \(T = T_0\); as \(t\) grows, \(e^{-kt} \to 0\) and \(T \to T_{\mathrm{env}}\). The model has three parameters, \(T_{\mathrm{env}}\), \(T_0\) and \(k\), each with a physical meaning.
The lesson: if you know the law, fit its parameters. With the right formula a parametric fit is the best you can do. Without a law, a flexible method may do better. The same cooling cup returns on the next page, fitted without using the law.
Flexibility versus interpretability# Methods placed by flexibility (horizontal axis) and interpretability (vertical axis), after ISLP. Top left: subset selection, the lasso and least squares, which are simple and easy to read. Middle: generalised additive models and trees. Bottom right: bagging, boosting, support vector machines and deep learning, which can fit almost anything but are hard to read. Two properties of a method pull in opposite directions:
Flexibility: how many different shapes of \(f\) the method can fit. Interpretability: how easily we can read what the model has learned. A straight line is inflexible but easy to read: its slope is a single number with a meaning. A deep neural network can fit almost any shape, but its millions of parameters have no individual meaning. (The method names in the chart are introduced in Lectures 2–7.)
How to choose:
For inference, choose a less flexible model, so that each parameter has a meaning you can check against physics. For prediction, a more flexible model may help, but not always: very flexible models can overfit, following the noise instead of \(f\). The next page shows this happening. Supervised and unsupervised; regression and classification# Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a category. In the notation of this page:
Supervised learning: every input \(x_i\) comes with a label \(y_i\). The goal is to predict \(y\) for new \(x\), or to understand how \(y\) depends on \(x\). Methods: linear and logistic regression, support vector machines, boosting, neural networks. Unsupervised learning: there are no \(y_i\). The goal is to find groups or structure among the \(x_i\). Methods: clustering, which finds groups, and principal components analysis (PCA), which finds the few combinations of inputs that carry most of the variation (Lecture 8). Supervised problems are further divided by the type of output:
Regression: \(y\) is quantitative, a number on a scale. Examples: the electricity use (kWh) of an area; the true temperature, predicted from the raw reading of a drifting sensor (and perhaps its age and the ambient temperature). Classification: \(y\) is qualitative, a category from a fixed list (also called a class). Examples: a machine is healthy or faulty; a milk sample is pure or adulterated, decided from its density, conductivity or spectrum. The boundary can blur. Logistic regression (Lecture 3) is a classification method, yet its output is the probability of a class, which is a number.

title: Assessing model accuracy
content:
Assessing model accuracy# How do we tell a good model from a bad one? This page introduces the standard score for regression, the mean squared error, and uses a cooling cup of tea to show the most important lesson in machine learning: a model must be judged on data it has not seen. That lesson leads to the bias–variance trade-off.
Notation on this page
Symbol Meaning \(y_i\) measured output of observation \(i\) \(\hat f(x_i)\) the model's prediction for observation \(i\) (also written \(\hat y_i\)) \(y_i - \hat f(x_i)\) the error (residual) of observation \(i\): measured minus predicted \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\) add over all \(n\) observations and divide by \(n\): the average MSE mean squared error; units of \(y\) squared (e.g. \(^\circ\)C\(^2\)) RMSE root mean squared error \(= \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}\); units of \(y\) \(\hat T\), \(t\) predicted temperature (\(^\circ\)C) and time (min) in the cooling example \(a_0, \dots, a_d\) the coefficients (parameters) of a polynomial \(d\) degree of a polynomial: its highest power \(x_0\), \(y_0\) a new input (not in the training data) and its measured output \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0))\) variance of the model: how much its prediction at \(x_0\) changes from one training set to another \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))\) bias of the model: its average prediction at \(x_0\) minus the true \(f(x_0)\) \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\) variance of the noise: the irreducible error The mean squared error# The residual of each point is the vertical distance to the fitted line. The mean of their squares is the MSE. For a regression model the standard score is the mean squared error:
\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - \hat f(x_i)\bigr)^2 . \]Read it from the inside out. \(\hat f(x_i)\) is the prediction for observation \(i\); \(y_i - \hat f(x_i)\) is its error, measured minus predicted; squaring makes every error positive; and \(\frac1n\sum\) averages over the \(n\) observations. A small MSE means the predictions lie close to the data.
Why square? Without squaring, positive and negative errors would cancel, and a terrible model could score zero. Squaring also punishes large errors most: an error of 3 counts nine times as much as an error of 1.
Example. Errors of \(+1\), \(-2\) and \(+3\) \(^\circ\)C give
\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1^2 + (-2)^2 + 3^2}{3} = \frac{1 + 4 + 9}{3} \approx 4.67\ ^\circ\mathrm C^2 . \]The MSE is in squared units. Its square root, the RMSE, is back in the units of \(y\) and reads as a typical error.
Example: the mean squared error by hand# A model predicts the temperature of a motor housing at five times. The measured and predicted values (°C) are
measured \(y_i\) 20.1 22.4 25.0 27.9 30.2 predicted \(\hat y_i\) 20.5 22.0 25.6 27.5 30.0 Compute the mean squared error and its square root (the RMSE). What are the units of each?
Solution triple-click to reveal Residuals \(y_i - \hat y_i\): -0.4, +0.4, -0.6, +0.4, +0.2. Their squares: 0.16, 0.16, 0.36, 0.16, 0.04.
\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{5}(0.16 + 0.16 + 0.36 + 0.16 + 0.04) = 0.176\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}^2, \qquad \mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{0.176} = 0.420\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}. \]The MSE is in squared units; the RMSE is back in °C, so it reads as a typical error of about 0.420 °C.
Example: fitting a cooling curve# A hot drink cools towards room temperature: a curve we know from physics. Photo: epSos.de, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 A temperature sensor in a cup of tea records 15 readings as the tea cools. The data are simulated from Newton's law of cooling, \(T = 25 + 60\,e^{-t/8}\) \(^\circ\)C (room temperature 25 \(^\circ\)C, starting temperature 85 \(^\circ\)C), plus random noise with standard deviation \(\sigma = 2\) \(^\circ\)C.
Now we pretend not to know the law, and fit polynomials in time instead:
\[ \hat T = a_0 + a_1 t + a_2 t^2 + \dots + a_d t^d . \]The degree \(d\) is the highest power of \(t\). A polynomial of degree \(d\) has \(d + 1\) coefficients \(a_0, \dots, a_d\), so a higher degree means a more flexible curve.
The same 15 readings fitted by polynomials of degree 1 (left), 3 (middle) and 12 (right). The straight line is too stiff and misses the curve. Degree 3 follows the cooling curve well. Degree 12 passes close to every point but wiggles wildly between them, especially near the end. Which fit would you trust to predict the temperature at \(t = 26\) min, just beyond the data? The degree-12 curve has the smallest error on the 15 readings, yet near 26 minutes it swings above 70 \(^\circ\)C, which is physically absurd for a cooling cup. Degree 3 is the sensible choice. The next section makes this judgement precise.
Training error versus test error# Keep some data aside: fit on the training data, judge on the test data. Two different MSEs can be computed for each fitted polynomial:
the training MSE, on the 15 readings used to fit the curve; the test MSE, on 1000 new readings the curve never saw. Training MSE (falls steadily) and test MSE (U-shaped) against the polynomial degree, 1 to 12. The vertical axis is logarithmic: each gridline is ten times the one below. The horizontal line marks the noise variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = 4\ ^\circ\mathrm C^2\). degree \(d\) training MSE (\(^\circ\)C\(^2\)) test MSE (\(^\circ\)C\(^2\)) 1 71.3 45.6 3 2.5 5.0 12 0.70 168 Four observations:
The training MSE always falls as flexibility grows. A more flexible model can always get at least as close to the training points: from 71 at degree 1 to 0.7 at degree 12. The test MSE falls, then rises: a U-shape. At first, extra flexibility captures the real curve better and the test MSE falls (46 at degree 1, 5.0 at degree 3). Beyond that, the extra flexibility fits the noise in the 15 training points. That noise does not repeat in new data, so the test MSE rises (168 at degree 12). The test MSE never goes below \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = 2^2 = 4\). This is the irreducible error of the previous page: even the true cooling law would have test MSE 4. The best polynomial, degree 3, reaches 5.0, close to this floor. A small training MSE with a large test MSE is overfitting. At degree 12 the training MSE (0.7) is even below the noise variance. That is a warning sign: the model is memorising the noise. Too simple, just right, too flexible. The rule that follows is the most important in machine learning: choose a model by its test error, not its training error. Lecture 4 shows how to estimate the test error when there is no separate test set (cross-validation).
The bias–variance decomposition# Bias: how far the average model is from the truth. Variance: how much the model changes from one data set to another. Why is the test error U-shaped? Imagine repeating the whole experiment many times. Each repeat gives a new set of 15 noisy readings, hence a different fitted curve, hence a different prediction at some fixed new time \(x_0\). The expected value \(\mathbb E\) below averages over all these repeats. The average squared error at \(x_0\) splits into three parts, all positive:
\[ \mathbb E\bigl(y_0 - \hat f(x_0)\bigr)^2 = \operatorname{Var}\bigl(\hat f(x_0)\bigr) + \bigl[\operatorname{Bias}\bigl(\hat f(x_0)\bigr)\bigr]^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon). \]Here \(y_0\) is the measured output at \(x_0\), and:
Variance, \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0))\): how much the prediction changes from one training set to another. A very flexible model follows every detail of its training data, so different training sets give very different curves: high variance. Bias, \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0)) = \mathbb E\hat f(x_0) - f(x_0)\): the average prediction minus the truth. It is the error from using a model that is too simple. A straight line cannot follow a curved cooling law however much data it is given; its average prediction is systematically off. Noise, \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\): the irreducible error, as before. As flexibility grows, bias falls and variance rises; the test error is lowest in between. Try it. Raise the polynomial degree. The training error always falls; the test error falls, then rises again: first bias goes down, then variance takes over. Underfitting and overfitting# A sketch (shapes only, not computed from data): squared bias falls and variance rises with flexibility. Their sum, plus the flat noise level, is the U-shaped test MSE. The decomposition names the two ways a model can fail:
High bias, low variance: underfitting. The model is too simple to follow \(f\), like the straight line on the cooling data. It is stable, but wrong. Low bias, high variance: overfitting. The model follows the noise, like the degree-12 polynomial. It is right on average, but unstable: each training set gives a wildly different curve. More flexibility lowers bias but raises variance. The best model balances the two, at the bottom of the U. The noise term cannot be reduced by any choice of model.

title: SVMs in practice
content:
SVMs in practice# This page covers SVMs with more than two classes, explains why SVMs and logistic regression so often give similar answers, and lists the practical points to watch.
Notation on this page
Symbol Meaning \(K\) number of classes \(f(x_i)\) the SVM's (or logistic regression's) linear score for point \(i\); its sign gives the class \(y_i\) class of point \(i\), coded \(+1\) or \(-1\) \(y_i f(x_i)\) signed distance: positive on the correct side, negative on the wrong side, large when far on the correct side hinge loss the SVM's loss, \(\max(0,\ 1 - y_i f(x_i))\): zero outside the street, rising in a straight line inside it log loss the loss of logistic regression (the cross-entropy of Lecture 3) More than two classes# An SVM separates two classes. For \(K\) classes there are two standard schemes:
One-versus-one: fit an SVM for every pair of classes, \(K(K - 1)/2\) SVMs in all. Each SVM votes, and the class with the most votes wins. scikit-learn's SVC does this. One-versus-all: fit \(K\) SVMs, each separating one class from all the others, and choose the class whose SVM is most confident (largest \(f(x)\)). For the fault type (imbalance, misalignment or bearing wear, \(K = 3\)) both need 3 SVMs (\(3 \times 2/2 = 3\) pairs). With 10 classes it would be 45 against 10.
SVMs and logistic regression# An SVM can be written as minimising a loss plus a ridge-like penalty on the coefficients (ISLP Section 9.5). Its loss is the hinge loss
\[ \max\bigl(0,\ 1 - y_i f(x_i)\bigr), \]where \(y_i f(x_i)\) is the signed distance of point \(i\): positive for a correctly classified point, and large when the point is far on the correct side. (The name comes from the shape of its graph, bent like a door hinge at \(y_i f(x_i) = 1\).)
The hinge loss of the SVM and the log loss of logistic regression, against the signed distance \(y_i f(x_i)\). Both penalise points on the wrong side heavily; the hinge loss is exactly zero for points safely outside the street (\(y_i f(x_i) \ge 1\)), while the log loss only approaches zero. The two losses have almost the same shape:
Both penalise points on the wrong side, roughly in proportion to how far they are. The SVM ignores points safely outside the street (loss exactly 0). That is why only the support vectors matter. The log loss is never exactly zero, so every point has a little influence. So the two methods usually give similar answers: on milk data set B the test errors were 0.177 (best SVM) and 0.176 (logistic regression). The practical difference is in the output: logistic regression gives probabilities; an SVM gives a class (and a distance from the boundary).
Things to watch# Standardise the inputs: kernels use distances. Tune \(C\) and \(\gamma\) together by cross-validation, over a grid. They interact: a large \(\gamma\) needs a smaller \(C\) to avoid overfitting. Know your library's \(C\): scikit-learn's \(C\) works in the opposite direction to ISLP's. Large data sets: kernel SVMs become slow beyond some tens of thousands of rows; training time grows roughly with the square of the number of rows, or worse. Probabilities: SVC(probability=True) estimates them with an extra step (fitting a sigmoid to the SVM distances by internal cross-validation, called Platt scaling). They are less reliable than those of logistic regression. Summary of Lecture 6# The maximal margin classifier finds the widest street between two classes. Only the support vectors decide the boundary. The soft margin allows overlap; \(C\) controls the width of the street (in scikit-learn, small \(C\) = wide). Kernels give curved boundaries by enlarging the feature space implicitly. SVMs and logistic regression often perform alike; kernels win when the boundary is curved.

title: When to use deep learning
content:
When to use deep learning# The three examples of this lecture show three different outcomes: networks lost on a table of sensor readings, won decisively on images, and helped modestly on a time series. This page draws the lessons.
Where deep learning shines, and where it does not# Deep learning needs graphics cards (GPUs) and a lot of data. Photo: Timothy Borkowski, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 Deep learning shines with:
images, sound, vibration signals and text; raw inputs where you do not know the right features; large data sets. Try simpler models first when:
the data are a table of measured features (on the six-sensor machines, the random forest won); the data set is small; you must be able to explain the model. Occam's razor (ISLP Section 10.6): if a simpler model does about as well, prefer it.
Predictive models: useful, within limits. xkcd #2169 “Predictive Models” by Randall Munroe, CC BY-NC 2.5. Hover for the alt text. Things to watch# Standardise the inputs. For images: subtract the mean pixel value and divide by the standard deviation. Keep a validation set for early stopping and for choosing the architecture (number of layers and units); keep the test set for the very end. Randomness: results change with the seed and with the library version. Fix the seed, and report the spread over a few seeds. Start small: a small network that trains beats a big one that does not. Hardware: small networks run on an ordinary processor (CPU). For large images use a graphics card (GPU); Google Colab offers one free (Runtime → Change runtime type → GPU; then move the model and data to "cuda" in PyTorch). Summary of Lecture 7# A neural network stacks linear models with non-linear activations between them. It is fitted by gradient descent, with gradients from backpropagation, in minibatches. Networks overfit easily: use dropout, weight decay or early stopping. Convolutional networks share small filters across an image; recurrent networks carry a memory along a sequence. On tables of features, try trees and linear models first.

title: Classification
content:
Classification# When the output is a category, the mean squared error no longer makes sense. This page introduces the error rate, the ideal (but unreachable) Bayes classifier, and a first practical method, \(K\)-nearest neighbours.
Notation on this page
Symbol Read as Meaning \(y_i\), \(\hat y_i\) true and predicted class of observation \(i\) \(\neq\) “is not equal to” \(I(\cdot)\) “indicator of …” 1 if the statement in brackets is true, 0 if false \(j\) a class, e.g. healthy or faulty \(\Pr(\cdot)\) “probability of …” a number between 0 and 1 \(\mid\) “given” \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)\): the probability that the class is \(j\), given that the input is \(x_0\) \(K\) the number of neighbours that vote in KNN \(\mathcal N_0\) “N nought” the set of the \(K\) training points nearest to \(x_0\) \(i \in \mathcal N_0\) “i in N nought” observation \(i\) is one of those neighbours The error rate# A portable vibration-measurement kit. Vibration levels are the inputs of our machine-fault examples. Photo: NotecA, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 For a category, “measured minus predicted” has no meaning: faulty minus healthy is not a number, so there is nothing to square. Instead we count the mistakes. The error rate is the fraction of wrong labels:
\[ \text{error rate} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} I\bigl(y_i \neq \hat y_i\bigr). \]\(I(\cdot)\) is the indicator function: it equals 1 if the statement in brackets is true and 0 if it is false. For each observation, \(I(y_i \neq \hat y_i)\) is 1 for a wrong label and 0 for a right one. The sum therefore counts the mistakes, and dividing by \(n\) turns the count into a fraction. The accuracy, the fraction labelled correctly, is one minus the error rate.
Example. A model labels 10 motors and gets 2 of them wrong. The error rate is \(2/10 = 0.2\) and the accuracy is \(1 - 0.2 = 0.8\).
As with the MSE, what matters is the test error rate, measured on new observations.
The Bayes classifier# Suppose we knew, for every possible input \(x_0\), the probability of each class: \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)\), read “the probability that the class is \(j\), given that the input is \(x_0\)”. The Bayes classifier assigns \(x_0\) to the class with the largest such probability.
It has the lowest error rate any classifier can achieve, called the Bayes error rate, because it always picks the most probable class. The Bayes error rate plays the role that the irreducible error \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) plays in regression: no classifier can beat it.
Example. A motor vibrates at 6 mm/s. Suppose that of all motors vibrating at 6 mm/s, 80% are faulty: \(\Pr(\text{faulty} \mid 6\text{ mm/s}) = 0.8\) and \(\Pr(\text{healthy} \mid 6\text{ mm/s}) = 0.2\). The Bayes classifier says faulty. Labelling all such motors faulty is wrong 20% of the time, and no rule that sees only the vibration level can do better.
In practice we never know these probabilities, so the Bayes classifier is an ideal to approach, not a method we can use. (In a simulation we choose the probabilities ourselves, so there we can compare a method against it.)
\(K\)-nearest neighbours (KNN)# KNN: find the K closest known machines and take a vote. The answer can depend on K. \(K\)-nearest neighbours estimates the unknown class probabilities from the training data near \(x_0\):
Find the \(K\) training points closest to \(x_0\). Call this set \(\mathcal N_0\). Estimate the probability of each class \(j\) by the fraction of these neighbours that belong to it: \[ \Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0) \approx \frac1K \sum_{i \in \mathcal N_0} I(y_i = j). \] The sum counts how many of the \(K\) neighbours are in class \(j\). Predict the most common class among the neighbours. Example. With \(K = 5\), suppose 4 of the 5 nearest motors are faulty. The indicator is 1 for the four faulty neighbours and 0 for the healthy one, so the sum is 4 and \(\Pr(\text{faulty}) \approx \tfrac15 \times 4 = 0.8\). Predict faulty.
Choosing \(K\). \(K\) controls the flexibility of the method.
Small \(K\) (1 or 3) gives a flexible, noisy boundary between the classes and may overfit. With \(K = 1\) each new point takes the label of its single nearest neighbour, so the boundary follows every noisy point. The training error is then zero (each training point is its own nearest neighbour), but the test error is not. Large \(K\) takes the vote over a wide region, which makes the boundary smooth, and possibly too smooth to follow the real shape: it may underfit. \(K\) plays the same role as the polynomial degree on the previous page, in reverse: a small \(K\) is flexible. As with the degree, \(K\) is chosen by the test error.
KNN is non-parametric: it keeps the training data and assumes no formula for \(f\).
Try it. Change \(K\). With \(K = 1\) the training error is 0 but the test error is high; a moderate \(K\) gives the lowest test error. Example: KNN by hand# Six machines have vibration levels (mm/s) and known states:
vibration 1.0 1.5 2.2 3.0 3.8 4.5 state healthy healthy faulty healthy faulty faulty Classify a new machine with vibration 2.5 mm/s using KNN with \(K = 1\) and with \(K = 3\).
Solution triple-click to reveal Distances from 2.5: 1 → 1.5, 1.5 → 1.0, 2.2 → 0.3, 3 → 0.5, 3.8 → 1.3, 4.5 → 2.0.
\(K = 1\): the nearest machine is at 2.2 (distance 0.3), which is faulty, so predict faulty. \(K = 3\): the three nearest are at 2.2, 3, 1.5: faulty, healthy, healthy. The majority is healthy. The prediction can change with \(K\): that is why \(K\) is chosen by checking the error on new data.
Summary of Lecture 1# Machine learning learns rules (a model) from data with known answers. Every method has three parts: representation, evaluation, optimisation. We assume \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) and estimate \(f\); the noise \(\varepsilon\) cannot be removed. Judge a model by its test error. Too simple underfits (high bias); too flexible overfits (high variance). Classification uses the error rate; KNN estimates class probabilities from the \(K\) nearest neighbours.

title: 1. Introduction to machine learning
content:
Lecture 1: Introduction to machine learning# What machine learning is, the notation of the course, and the ideas that every later lecture builds on: the model \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\), training and test error, the bias–variance trade-off, and a first classifier.
Contents# What is machine learning?: definitions, why we need it, the three ingredients of every method, vocabulary, types of learning. Notation and matrix algebra: data as a matrix, the transpose and the matrix product. Statistical learning: expected value and variance; \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\); reducible and irreducible error; parametric and non-parametric methods. Assessing model accuracy: the mean squared error, training versus test error, bias and variance. Classification: the error rate, the Bayes classifier, \(K\)-nearest neighbours. You will need# Basic Python, and the mathematics listed on the home page. Every symbol is explained where it first appears, and each page starts with a table of the notation it uses.
