title: 2. Linear regression
content:
Lecture 2: Linear regression# Fitting straight lines and planes to data, judging how far to trust the result, and training a model step by step with gradient descent. The examples are the calibration of a temperature sensor, the power of a solar panel, and a discharging capacitor.
Contents# Simple linear regression: least squares; standard error, \(t\), \(p\); RSE and \(R^2\). Multiple linear regression: many inputs; matrix form and the normal equations; dummy variables; interactions; straightening curves; checking residuals. Gradient descent: loss and cost; the gradient; step size; standardising inputs. You will need# Lecture 1, especially the notation and the mean squared error, and derivatives from calculus (partial derivatives are explained where they are used).

title: 3. Classification
content:
Lecture 3: Classification# Predicting a category instead of a number: is a machine healthy or faulty? This lecture develops logistic regression, shows how to judge a classifier and choose its threshold, and introduces the generative classifiers LDA, QDA and naive Bayes.
Contents# Logistic regression: the sigmoid; odds and log-odds; likelihood and maximum likelihood; cross-entropy; gradient descent; decision boundaries. How good is a classifier?: the confusion matrix; accuracy, recall, precision, specificity; choosing the threshold; the ROC curve and AUC. Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes: Bayes' theorem; the three methods; comparing classifiers; more than two classes. You will need# Lecture 1 (training and test error, the Bayes classifier, KNN) and Lecture 2 (coefficients, standard errors, loss and cost, gradient descent, standardising inputs).

title: 4. Resampling and regularisation
content:
Lecture 4: Resampling and regularisation# How well will a model do on data it has never seen, when all we have is one data set? And how do we stop a model with many inputs from fitting the noise? This lecture answers both: cross-validation and the bootstrap, then ridge regression and the lasso.
Contents# Resampling: the validation set; leave-one-out and \(k\)-fold cross-validation; the bootstrap. Regularisation: too many inputs; subset selection; ridge regression; the lasso; choosing \(\lambda\) by cross-validation. You will need# From Lecture 1: the MSE, training and test error, overfitting, bias and variance. From Lecture 2: least squares, standard errors, standardising inputs. The bootstrap example uses the logistic regression of Lecture 3.

title: 5. Non-linear models and trees
content:
Lecture 5: Non-linear models and trees# Models that find the shape of a relationship from the data, instead of us choosing it: splines and generalised additive models for smooth curves, and decision trees and their ensembles (bagging, random forests, boosting) for thresholds and interactions.
Contents# Beyond straight lines: polynomials and step functions; regression splines; choosing the knots; smoothing splines and local regression; GAMs. Tree-based methods: growing and pruning a tree; bagging; random forests; boosting; variable importance. You will need# From earlier lectures: residuals, overfitting and the variance of a model (Lecture 1), least squares (Lecture 2), test error and AUC (Lecture 3), and cross-validation, the bootstrap and penalties (Lecture 4).

title: 6. Support vector machines
content:
Lecture 6: Support vector machines# A classifier that looks for the widest gap between the classes, allows for overlap, and bends the gap into curves with kernels. It is developed in the three steps of ISLP Chapter 9: the maximal margin classifier (separable classes), the support vector classifier (overlapping classes), and the support vector machine (curved boundaries).
Contents# The maximal margin classifier: hyperplanes; the margin; support vectors. The support vector classifier: the soft margin; slack; the cost \(C\) and its two conventions. Kernels: enlarging the feature space; linear, polynomial and radial kernels. SVMs in practice: more than two classes; SVMs and logistic regression; things to watch. You will need# Decision boundaries and the log loss (Lecture 3); standardising inputs, bias and variance, and tuning hyperparameters by cross-validation (Lectures 1–4).

title: 7. Neural networks and deep learning
content:
Lecture 7: Neural networks and deep learning# Networks that learn their own features from raw inputs: fully connected networks and how they are trained (backpropagation), convolutional networks for images, recurrent networks for sequences, and when deep learning is worth using.
Contents# Neural networks: hidden units and activations; many layers; fitting and backpropagation; overfitting and regularisation. Convolutional networks: convolution and shared weights; pooling; thermal images of circuit boards. Recurrent networks: hidden state and memory; forecasting electricity demand. When to use deep learning: where it shines; things to watch.
